item.title: HERMES and Mercury, open-source systems for sending email over shortwave radio
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: HERMES, built by the nonprofit Rhizomatica, lets communities without mobile signal or internet access exchange email and files over shortwave radio, and Mercury, a modem released in May, has made the whole system open source. Anyone within range can receive a radio signal, and the rules on encryption over amateur radio differ by country. As of 23 November, amateur radio operators in Taiwan may not communicate in code words or ciphers without the regulator's approval, and those in mainland China must communicate in plain language or recognised amateur abbreviations, using public protocols.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 9 sources, including ARDC, IEEE Spectrum, Rhizomatica

Where there is no mobile signal or internet access, shortwave (HF) radio can carry a signal several hundred kilometres. Rhizomatica, a nonprofit working to bring communications to underserved communities, developed HERMES so that people without much radio or technical experience can send and receive messages, email and files over shortwave. In May, Rhizomatica released Mercury, an open-source modem (software that turns data into signals a radio can transmit). According to a write-up published on 6 November by ARDC, an amateur radio foundation that funds the project, Mercury replaces VARA, a proprietary modem that required a paid license for every radio, and with it the whole of HERMES is now open source.

Shortwave signals are reflected by the ionosphere in the upper atmosphere, so they can reach places where ground infrastructure is hard to build. In an interview with IEEE Spectrum, Rhizomatica's founder said they use small radios with an output of about 20 watts, and can link two radios 400 to 600 kilometres apart fairly reliably. The trade-off is speed. According to the same article, typical shortwave radios carry digital data at only a few hundred bits per second.

In an article on the Public Interest Technology Group website, the founder wrote that HERMES first compresses the data and then passes email along with UUCP, an early protocol designed to cope with interrupted connections. According to the project manual, a gateway station (the point where the shortwave network meets the internet) is usually set up somewhere with internet access, and each community with no other means of communication gets a remote station.

The largest HERMES deployment has nearly 90 radios, and according to ARDC's write-up some of the sites take days to reach on foot or by boat. Rhizomatica works with local partners and concentrates training on a small group of community members, with the aim that communities install, operate and maintain the system themselves. In the interview, the founder described a pilot project that put HERMES on 10 or 11 fishing boats, one of which broke down 100 or 200 kilometres offshore. He said the crew used HERMES to send their GPS position and a distress message, and both the crew and the boat were rescued.

According to ARDC, Mercury can also be used on its own, without HERMES, so amateur radio operators can connect it to their own radios. Some operators are already using it to exchange email, and have reported bugs and contributed changes.

Perspective

Anyone with a receiver within range can pick up a radio signal, and on shortwave that range can stretch to hundreds of kilometres. In October The New Yorker reported on a rural tradition of passing private messages over AM radio stations, where the messages are often worded vaguely because anyone can hear what is broadcast.

In his Public Interest Technology Group article, the founder argues that with shortwave it is hard to tell where a signal is coming from, and harder still to know who is receiving it. He explained in the IEEE Spectrum interview that the rules on encryption for amateur radio differ by country, which is why encryption in HERMES can be switched on or off. The encryption was built in because some of Rhizomatica's partners are in very sensitive areas and do not want to send information that can easily be intercepted and used against them. The signal itself can still be recorded by anyone, though, and since Mercury's source code is public, whoever records it could in principle use the same software to recover any data that was not encrypted.

Amateur radio in Taiwan is governed by the Regulations Governing Amateur Radio Operators and Stations, issued by the National Communications Commission (NCC) in 2020. As of 23 November, the regulations prohibit amateur radio operators from communicating in code words or ciphers that the competent authority has not approved while operating an amateur station. Under this rule, HERMES cannot be used on Taiwan's amateur bands with encryption switched on unless approval has been obtained.

Mainland China's Measures for the Administration of Amateur Radio Stations (MIIT Order No. 67), issued by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and in force since 1 March 2024, limit amateur stations to communicating with one another, technical research and self-training, and bar their use for commercial gain. As of 23 November, the measures also require operators to communicate in plain language or in abbreviations and shorthand recognised in amateur radio, using public technical systems and communication protocols. Encrypted content is not plain language, so going by the republished text of the measures, switching on HERMES's encryption on mainland China's amateur bands may not meet this requirement, although the measures do not mention encryption by name.

Readers who can get online do not need this system. Licensed amateur radio operators who want to try HF data communication can start with Mercury. Its source code is on GitHub, the project page lists support for Linux (including Raspberry Pi) and Windows, and as of 23 November the latest release was v1.9.25, published on 21 November. Anyone trying it on amateur bands in Taiwan or mainland China should treat whatever they send as a public message that anyone within range can receive.

item.title: South Korea's biodata bill and the dispute over research use of health data
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: As of 22 November, South Korea's National Assembly was still reviewing a biodata bill that would let research institutions and researchers use pseudonymized portions of genetic and clinical data for AI biotech research without the consent of the people concerned. Supporters say researchers can wait up to 18 months for data, while six medical, patient and social welfare groups, concerned about use without consent and a single consolidated review, issued a statement on 18 November calling for the bill to be scrapped. The Health and Welfare Committee is reviewing a separate health data bill put forward by the government at the same time.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 13 sources, including 국회입법예고, 디지털정의네트워크, 대한민국 정책브리핑

South Korea's National Assembly Science, ICT, Broadcasting and Communications Committee (과학기술정보방송통신위원회, the science committee) is reviewing two biodata bills. At the same time, the Health and Welfare Committee (보건복지위원회) is reviewing a government version of the Digital Healthcare Act (디지털헬스케어법) put forward by the Ministry of Health and Welfare (보건복지부). The Bill on the Use of Biodata and the Promotion of AI-Bio Research and Development (바이오데이터 활용 및 인공지능바이오 연구개발 촉진에 관한 법률안, hereafter the biodata bill), introduced by lawmakers in December 2025, had not passed as of 22 November and is waiting for review by the science committee's bill review subcommittee. If it passes, research institutions and researchers could use pseudonymized portions of genetic and clinical data for AI biotech research without the consent of the people the data describe.

Supporters of the bill argue that getting access to data takes too long. Reporting on a forum held to push for the law, the Korean daily Electronic Times (전자신문) wrote that data from rare-disease patients can take up to 18 months to reach researchers. Six medical, patient and social welfare groups are concerned about use without consent and about a single consolidated review, and on 18 November they published a statement calling for both biodata bills to be scrapped.

Under the biodata bill, the Minister of Science and ICT, who heads the Ministry of Science and ICT (과학기술정보통신부, MSIT), could build a national integrated biodata system and request data from public bodies such as the National Health Insurance Service (국민건강보험공단). The data must be pseudonymized before they are handed over, meaning fields such as names are replaced with codes, which differs from anonymization, where the person can no longer be identified at all. Article 23 lists what may be used without consent, including partial genetic information that cannot identify an individual on its own, and clinical, environmental and other data about unspecified individuals or groups. A presidential decree (an executive order) can add further items, and data that could easily be combined with other information to identify someone are excluded.

Article 21 sets up a research review committee to carry out a single consolidated review. It has up to 20 members appointed or commissioned by the Minister of Science and ICT, including people recommended by the Minister of Health and Welfare and by the Chair of South Korea's Personal Information Protection Commission (개인정보보호위원회, PIPC, the country's data protection authority). Matters this committee has reviewed are deemed to have undergone the review required by the Bioethics and Safety Act (생명윤리 및 안전에 관한 법률), that is, the research ethics review carried out by each institution's institutional review board (IRB). Articles 21 and 23 appear only in the bill introduced in December 2025, and according to the statement, the other bill removes these provisions.

Article 4 provides that, except where other laws contain special provisions, the use of biodata and AI-bio research and development are governed by this Act. According to the statement, the PIPC is concerned that if the Act were applied ahead of the Personal Information Protection Act (개인정보 보호법), the existing system of protections would be weakened.

In the statement, the groups also criticize the government's bill for using pseudonymized data without consent, but argue that health data should at least be debated within the legal framework for health and medical care. Medigate News, a Korean medical news outlet, reported that the health ministry and the Democratic Party of Korea aim to pass the government bill by the end of 2026.

Perspective

Pseudonymization removes the fields that identify someone directly, but each person's records stay linked to one another. Research needs that linkage, and the risk of re-identification comes from the same place. In October, the Korean outlet NoCut News reported that a health ministry official, speaking about the biodata bill, said it is hard to claim that pseudonymization alone removes every identification risk.

The Electronic Times reported on 19 October that the health ministry takes a cautious position on gathering treatment information in one place, and on the overlap with the functions of existing IRBs and data review boards (DRBs, committees that decide whether data can be released). According to the same report, MSIT considers legislation necessary to promote AI research and plans to keep talking with the health ministry.

Article 23 of the biodata bill only sets out what may be used, and the debate over opt-out (data are included by default, and individuals can ask to be excluded) has focused on the government bill. In a July 2025 ruling, the Supreme Court (대법원) held that individuals cannot demand a halt to pseudonymization carried out for scientific research, statistics or archiving in the public interest. Citing that ruling, the health ministry explained that the government bill follows the framework of the existing Personal Information Protection Act, while separately requiring consent for information with a high risk of re-identification, such as data on rare diseases.

At a National Assembly forum on the government bill on 2 November, a researcher from a public health research group argued that opt-out should be guaranteed, and a division director at the health ministry said an opt-out mechanism needed to be considered. At a public hearing on the Digital Healthcare Act, a representative of the Korean Medical Association (대한의사협회) also noted that once medical data are used to train AI, they are very hard to take back.

Under the biodata bill, the Article 21 committee carries out a single consolidated review, and according to the statement, the health ministry opposed this on the grounds that it could undermine bioethics safeguards. Under the government bill, review is handled by each agency's own review committee, whose members, according to the health ministry's explanation, include representatives of the people whose data are used and outside members. An Electronic Times reporter wrote that research is delayed because researchers must apply separately for an IRB exemption and for DRB review, and both committees take a conservative line and repeatedly ask for more documents.

According to its official documentation, the UK's OpenSAFELY keeps data with the organizations that already hold it. Researchers send their analysis code into a secure zone there to run, and results are released only after review. The biodata bill instead gathers the data into the integrated system first.

Both biodata bills are still under review, and readers do not need to do anything for now. Developments to watch are when the science committee's bill review subcommittee takes up the bills, and whether the government bill passes by the end of 2026.

In Taiwan, the Constitutional Court's Judgment 111-Hsien-Pan-13 of 2022 concerned the National Health Insurance Administration providing National Health Insurance data to government agencies and academic research institutions for uses beyond the original purpose. The court held that the lack of any way for people to ask for this to stop violated Article 22 of the Constitution, and gave the authorities three years to enact or amend legislation. The National Health Insurance Data Management Act (全民健康保險資料管理條例), promulgated in December 2025, provides for requests to stop such uses of all or part of a person's data, and leaves the date it takes effect to the Executive Yuan. A stop does not apply retroactively, so uses that took place before the request are unaffected.

According to Japan's Personal Information Protection Commission (PPC), the country's Act on the Protection of Personal Information requires consent, with exceptions, both to acquire sensitive information such as medical history and to provide personal data to third parties. An amendment promulgated on 17 July 2026, to take effect within two years of promulgation, removes the requirement for individual consent for providing personal data to third parties, and for acquiring sensitive information that has already been made public, when the data are used only to produce statistics, which in the PPC's explanation includes AI development that can be treated as producing statistics. Both parties must publish what they will do and agree in writing to use the data only for that purpose, and they are barred from using the data for anything else or passing them on. In our reading, once in force the amendment would, like the Korean biodata bill, allow use without individual consent, but only for producing statistics and under a written agreement between the parties, whereas Taiwan's Act lets individuals ask for use beyond the original purpose to stop.

When comparing systems in different places, readers can ask who can get the data, whether the data are centralized, whether individuals can refuse, and what happens to data that have already been used. They can also ask who appoints the reviewers, and whether the system can shorten the time researchers wait for data.

item.title: CircumVolve, a study using large language models to search for censorship evasion strategies
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Researchers had a large language model repeatedly rewrite circumvention programs and, testing on networks in China, Iran, Pakistan and Kazakhstan, found 47 strategies that get past censorship equipment, though a strategy that works in one country does not necessarily work in another. The strategies reach users only after tool developers build them into their tools, and ordinary readers do not need to change any settings.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 5 sources from GFW Report, GitHub

When a censor switches to a new way of blocking, the ways around it are still mostly found by researchers working by hand. They analyse blocking incidents, guess at what triggers them, hand-craft an evasion and test it, a cycle that, according to the paper, often takes weeks or months. On 16 November the GFW Report website published CircumVolve, a paper for the ACM CCS 2026 security conference, in which researchers had a large language model (LLM) repeatedly rewrite circumvention programs and tested the results in a simulated environment and on networks in China, Iran, Pakistan and Kazakhstan. According to the paper, it is meant as a discovery tool for circumvention researchers and tool developers, and ordinary readers do not need to change any settings.

A circumvention strategy is a change to the way packets or a protocol are written, so that censorship equipment cannot match a connection to a blocked site while the server still responds normally. The researchers write each strategy as an executable Python program, have the LLM produce variants over and over, and keep the versions that test well for further rounds of changes. The process is built on OpenEvolve, an open-source framework for evolving programs, and in each round the LLM proposes changes based on the score, the packets decoded into text, and any error messages. A strategy scores highly only if it both evades the censor and gets a correct response from the destination server, which stops the LLM from taking shortcuts such as deleting the blocked domain.

Existing automated tools can also search for circumvention strategies, for example Geneva, published in 2019. As the paper describes them, these tools combine packet operations according to fixed rules and cannot change what is inside encrypted protocols such as TLS (the encryption protocol HTTPS uses) and QUIC (a newer transport protocol for the web). The LLM writes ordinary Python code, which can handle the encryption within the program and so change the contents of encrypted protocols.

On a real network, researchers only learn whether a bypass succeeded or failed. The simulated environment uses OpenGFW, open-source software that simulates a censor, in place of real censorship equipment, so the researchers can trace why a strategy works. Strategies were also tested on datacenter VPSs (rented virtual servers) under the researchers' own control in censored regions, across five protocols: DNS (the lookup that turns domain names into IP addresses), TCP/IP, HTTP, TLS and QUIC. Each protocol was tested in two or three of the countries, chosen by how each country actually blocks it, and all experiments in Iran were completed before the nationwide internet shutdown there on 28 February 2026.

The researchers used CircumVolve to find 47 distinct strategies across the five protocols, 27 of which are, to the authors' knowledge, not documented in earlier work. At least one bypass was found for every protocol tested in every country, but a strategy does not necessarily work everywhere, and the authors "did not expect any strategy to work universally". In runs that did find a bypass, the median LLM API cost before the first successful evasion was less than US$1. The limitations the authors acknowledge include using a single model, GPT-5.1, for all experiments, and rewriting only the first packet of a connection for QUIC and TLS.

Perspective

In the ethics section, the authors argue that "censors must perfectly parse all protocols while evaders need only one overlooked edge case." With CircumVolve, the researchers hand the large number of attempts needed to find such edge cases to an LLM, which can adjust the next round of changes to how the censorship equipment responded. The authors suggest that some of the DNS strategies could be difficult to discover through fuzzing (testing with randomly varied inputs) alone.

The system relies on researchers who know censorship well to define the evaluation criteria and design the prompts, and automated deployment is listed in the paper as future work. Researchers who want to run it themselves have to supply their own VPS and LLM API keys. The authors also warn that testing sends malformed packets from the vantage point, so the testing activity itself may be recognised by the censor.

The authors have released the code, prompts and successful strategies, but as of 22 November the root of the CircumVolve repository had no license file, and only the bundled openevolve/ directory is under Apache-2.0. The terms for other projects that want to reuse the rest of the code directly are unclear.

On 18 November another research team introduced obfsgen on net4people, a discussion forum hosted on GitHub. obfsgen also uses a generative model, in this case to reshape the packet sizes and timing of encrypted tunnel traffic so that it resembles ordinary traffic. It is released under the MIT license, and it is marked in its README as not yet ready for production use.

In the ethics section the authors acknowledge that publication "may help censors identify and mitigate discovered strategies before circumvention tools deploy them." They publish anyway because "well-resourced censors can independently identify these techniques", and because, according to earlier research the paper cites, censors take some time (for example several months) to bring new techniques into their production systems. Given the low cost the paper reports and the release of the code and prompts, our reading is that a censor could test its own equipment the same way without much difficulty.

China, Pakistan and Kazakhstan all block QUIC connections by SNI (the name of the site being requested, carried in the first message of a TLS or QUIC connection), though not all in the same way. China began decrypting and inspecting the SNI of QUIC connections at scale in April 2024, and there the offending packet is allowed through while the packets that follow are dropped, according to the paper. Kazakhstan and Pakistan are, in the paper's words, "both consumers of China's censorship equipment exports". In both countries the equipment sits in the path of traffic, drops the offending packet and keeps blocking the connection afterwards.

According to the paper, researchers uncover evasion techniques "that developers subsequently deploy in the wild", so users get the new strategies only after their circumvention tools are updated. Until then, readers who use circumvention tools do not need to change any settings. The study targets censorship equipment that matches standard protocols against rules, and it did not test fully encrypted protocols, where the whole connection looks like random data, or proprietary protocols.

item.title: The breach of Japanese marketing platform KARTE and member data from hundreds of companies
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: KARTE, a marketing platform run by the Japanese company PLAID, Inc., was broken into by an outside attacker on 13 November. PLAID's investigation findings of 20 November list member data imported by hundreds of companies, and records of visitors' behaviour on those companies' websites, as leaked or possibly leaked, including data from companies whose contracts had ended and whose data should already have been deleted. Ordinary visitors may not know that a website uses KARTE. Customers and members of these companies, and users of their websites and apps, can watch for notices from the companies.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 13 sources, including PLAID, MUFG Bank, DHC

People who have signed up as members on a Japanese shopping site or banking app may have their data stored at a marketing company they have never dealt with directly. KARTE is a marketing platform from the Japanese company PLAID, Inc. that is embedded in companies' websites and apps to record what visitors view and click, and companies also import their own member data into KARTE to use alongside those records. PLAID detected an outside attacker on 13 November and shut down the entire KARTE service the same day, and its investigation findings published on 20 November list data entrusted by hundreds of companies as leaked or possibly leaked. Only customers and members of companies that have used KARTE, and people who have used those companies' websites or apps, can fall within the scope of this breach.

According to PLAID's announcement of 16 November, the attacker exploited a vulnerability in PLAID's servers in the early hours of the 13th to steal the credentials used to connect to its databases, and read data out of them. The attacker then used the same credentials to take over accounts and log in to KARTE's admin console, and PLAID detected the intrusion that morning and shut down its servers in the afternoon.

The 20 November announcement sorts the data that companies entrusted to KARTE into four categories, and because some companies fall into more than one, the per-category counts cannot be added up; the announcement gives no overall total. The two categories that concern website users directly are customer data the companies imported, such as member data (570 companies), and records of visitors' page views and clicks (487 companies), and in each case it is part of that data that leaked or may have leaked. The other two are cached data that KARTE held temporarily, which includes visitor identifiers, and credentials for connecting to services such as email delivery, the equivalent of keys or passwords. The credentials contain no personal data, but if they are not revoked they could be used to access those services.

The affected companies also include ones whose contracts with PLAID had fully or partly ended, a correction the 20 November announcement made to what PLAID said on 16 November. Under the terms of service this data should have been deleted when the contracts ended, but it remained because of lapses in staff operations and management, and PLAID plans to delete it and send notifications once the verification it will carry out for resuming the service is complete.

Company notices began appearing on 17 November, and by 21 November the Japanese security blog piyolog had listed 108 organisations that had published one. What leaked varies widely from company to company, and the two examples below are ones whose original notices we checked. MUFG Bank's notice covers about 6.5 million records containing only customers' gender, age and area of residence, with no names or contact details. DHC's covers about 19.11 million records, including names, email addresses, dates of birth and member IDs, but not login passwords or credit card data.

Perspective

KARTE's tracking tag is a piece of code that a company issues from the admin console and places on its web pages, and according to the developer documentation, once a visitor's browser loads it, the tag sends browsing events to KARTE. Companies separately import their own member data, so both kinds of data sit on the same platform, and data from hundreds of companies is concentrated with a single provider. The netiCRM incident we covered on 19 November was also a break-in at a service provider's server, after which one client organisation announced it had been notified that its donation database had been copied.

Visitors never sign up for KARTE themselves, and their data is handled by PLAID on behalf of the companies. PLAID's FAQ for ordinary visitors says it cannot answer whether a particular website uses KARTE or whether a given person's data is within the scope of the leak, and its announcements offer no way to look this up. To find out whether you are affected, you have to wait for a company's notice or ask the companies you deal with, and whether and when to notify is up to each company. Since data from companies whose contracts had ended was still on PLAID's systems, our reading is that data may also stay with the provider after a company stops using KARTE, and a request to delete it likewise goes to the company.

Content-blocking extensions can reduce the behavioural data that third-party tools collect in the browser, and filter lists such as EasyPrivacy can be applied to decide which addresses to block. The 21 November version of EasyPrivacy has blocking rules for only some KARTE addresses and also makes exceptions for 3 websites, so installing an extension does not guarantee that every request to KARTE is blocked. Extensions work only inside the browser and have no effect on collection inside apps. Member data is data a company already holds and imports into KARTE itself, so blocking KARTE's code in the browser does not stop the company from sending data it already has.

People who receive a notice from a company can check in it which items leaked, and the notices from MUFG Bank and DHC both say the companies will contact affected customers individually. DHC's notice asks customers who receive suspicious emails claiming to be from DHC not to open links or attachments, and not to enter personal data or passwords. Following these reminders lowers the chance of being tricked into handing over data by impersonation emails, but data that has already leaked cannot be taken back.

Japan's national data protection regulator is the Personal Information Protection Commission (PPC). Under Article 26(1) of the Act on the Protection of Personal Information, as in force on 9 October 2026, a business that handles personal data on another business's behalf need not report a breach to the PPC itself if it has notified the business that entrusted it with the data in the manner the PPC's rules set. Article 26(2) also excludes a business that has given such notice from the duty to notify the people affected, so in our reading, where PLAID has notified its clients in this way, telling customers falls to each client company.

JINS Japan is among the companies that issued notices, and according to iThome, JINS in Taiwan announced on 18 November that the leak was limited to systems in Japan and that Taiwanese members' data is managed separately and was not affected. In Taiwan, Article 12 of the Personal Data Protection Act as in force on 9 October 2026 requires an organisation that violates the Act, resulting in personal data being stolen or leaked, to notify the people concerned by appropriate means once the facts are established, but sets no deadline and no duty to report to a regulator, and amendments promulgated in November 2025 that add a reporting duty had no effective date as of that day. Reporting comes instead from sector rules, such as those of the Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC), which require banks and other financial institutions to report serious incidents within 72 hours. In mainland China, Article 57 of the Personal Information Protection Law requires a personal information handler, when personal information has been or may have been leaked, to take remedial measures immediately and notify the responsible authorities and the individuals concerned, with no set number of days, though individuals need not be notified if the measures can effectively prevent harm, unless the authorities consider harm possible and require notification.

PLAID has set mid-January 2027 as its target for resuming KARTE in stages, will also bring in a third-party organisation for verification, and plans to hand detailed data to each company in turn from 24 November. As of 22 November, the PPC had not posted anything about the incident on its website, while PLAID's announcement says it is in the process of reporting to the commission. Things to watch are whether companies update the number of records and the items in their notices once they have the detailed data, and how the commission handles the case.

item.title: Conditions and disputes over alternative browser engines on iOS in the EU and Japan
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: The EU and Japan require Apple to allow browser engines other than WebKit on iOS, and Apple has set conditions on security and privacy grounds. Mozilla writes that these conditions have kept it from launching a Gecko-based Firefox, and according to its 20 November post no developer had launched a non-WebKit iOS browser by then.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 9 sources, including Mozilla, Apple, Japan Fair Trade Commission

Every browser on the iPhone and iPad, whether Safari, Chrome, Firefox or one marketed on privacy, runs on Apple's WebKit engine (the core component that parses and displays web pages). Laws in the EU and Japan require Apple to allow other engines, and Apple has set conditions in both places on security and privacy grounds. In a post on 20 November, Mozilla writes that these conditions have so far kept it from launching a Firefox built on its own engine, and that not one developer had launched a non-WebKit browser on iOS by the time of the post. Apple's App Review Guidelines require apps that browse the web to use WebKit, and the conditions for an exception are set out on two separate pages, one for the EU and one for Japan.

According to Mozilla's post, iPhones and iPads are the only major platforms with this restriction. On Apple's own macOS, people can use the version of Firefox built on Gecko, the browser engine Mozilla develops. Many of Firefox's features are built into Gecko, which is why Mozilla cannot easily bring the full Firefox to the iPhone.

According to a summary by the advocacy group Open Web Advocacy (OWA), the EU's Digital Markets Act (DMA) requires large platforms designated as gatekeepers to allow other browser engines, an obligation Apple has had to meet since March 2024. Japan's Act on Promotion of Competition for Specified Smartphone Software (Mobile Software Competition Act, MSCA) has a similar provision. In the outline of the act published by the Japan Fair Trade Commission (JFTC), providers that exceed a size threshold and are designated by the JFTC "must not prevent other application developers from using other browser engines, for example, by imposing conditions that only allow the use of designated providers' proprietary browser engines". Exceptions are allowed where there are justifiable reasons such as security and privacy.

Under Apple's developer documentation, a developer who wants to use another engine must first be authorised by Apple, and the app can only be distributed in the EU or in Japan (the Japan conditions were published in December 2025). On security, vulnerabilities that are already being exploited must be mitigated "in a timely manner", and the example given in the documentation is "30 days for the simplest classes of vulnerabilities being actively exploited". On privacy, the engine must block third-party cookies (cookies that can be used to track people across websites) by default.

According to Mozilla, using Gecko would mean it could not simply update the Firefox app people already have, and would instead have to build "a whole separate app, a second Firefox". Users would then have to download the new app, move their bookmarks, passwords and history across, and switch over by hand. Mozilla writes that "[a] significant proportion of people would understandably give up, including many who picked Firefox from the EU's choice screen". One of the conditions bars Mozilla from disclosing non-public information about the project, but it still gave this example of what it is up against.

Browser engines constantly handle untrusted and potentially malicious content and have visibility of sensitive user data, which, according to Apple's developer documentation, makes them "one of the most common attack vectors for bad actors". Apple therefore only authorises developers who meet specific criteria and commit to ongoing security and privacy requirements. As quoted by OWA, Apple's vice president for legal said at a 2025 DMA workshop that third parties such as Google and Mozilla are able to bring their own engines, adding, "for whatever reason, they have chosen not to do so".

In a May post, OWA wrote that no browser vendor had brought its own engine to iOS in the EU, and asked the European Commission to investigate whether Apple is complying with the DMA in practice. As of 22 November we had found no Commission decision on Apple's browser engine conditions, and no public response from Apple to Mozilla's post.

The UK's Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) designated Apple's mobile platform as having strategic market status in October 2025, with the designation covering mobile browsers and browser engines. Following the designation, the CMA can impose targeted measures on Apple. On the CMA's programme of work page as of 22 November, work on Apple "concerning browsers (removal of the WebKit restriction)" is among the things the CMA expects to progress next, with no timetable given.

Perspective

Switching to another browser on iOS changes the interface, the default settings and the extra features, but the engine is WebKit every time. As this site's 14 November article on Tor options for the iPhone set out from the Tor Project's documentation, Tor Browser is built on Firefox's Gecko, and Onion Browser on the iPhone (an open-source browser that connects through the Tor onion routing network) cannot offer the same protection because of WebKit's limits. The built-in ad blocker in Firefox for iOS, covered in October, is likewise built on WebKit's content blocking technology, while Firefox on desktop and Android can install extensions directly.

Our reading of the local-distribution condition is that even if browsers with other engines appear in the EU or Japan, iPhone users in Taiwan, Hong Kong and elsewhere would still get WebKit browsers from the App Store. The exceptions would be separate permission from Apple, or a local law that also requires other engines to be allowed. The plan for an iOS Tor Browser covered in the 14 November article would face the same condition if it were distributed through the App Store.

Japan is the only place in Asia covered by Apple's alternative engine programmes, from iOS 26.2 onwards. According to Mozilla, no developer had launched a non-WebKit browser there either, almost a year after Apple published its Japan conditions. The conditions on Apple's Japan page match the EU page item by item, except that they cover iOS only, not iPadOS, allow distribution elsewhere only where "expressly permitted by Apple", and limit embedded engines for in-app browsing to browser engine stewards (organisations primarily responsible for operating an engine). Everywhere else, the App Review Guidelines require WebKit and list exceptions only for the EU and Japan, so going by the text of the guidelines, the same rule applies in mainland China, Taiwan and Hong Kong, and as of 22 November no local law requiring Apple to allow other engines could be found in any of the three.

Apple's two public pages of conditions include security and privacy requirements and the local-distribution limit, but no wording about building a separate app. Mozilla, for its part, writes that a confidentiality condition prevents it from disclosing the details. On why no browser has launched, Mozilla and OWA point to Apple's conditions, while Apple's vice president for legal, at the 2025 workshop, pointed to the vendors' own choice.

Anyone who needs to browse through Tor on an iPhone can use Onion Browser, covered in the 14 November article, together with Orbot (an app that sends the phone's connections into the Tor network). Pages are handled by WebKit in this setup too, and according to the same article, very little can be adjusted against browser fingerprinting (identifying visitors from details of their device and browser). Tor Browser exists only for desktop and Android, so anyone who needs its full protection has to use one of those devices, and the same goes for anyone who wants Firefox extensions. Readers who only use Safari or another browser have nothing to change now.

In comparing how different places handle this, Apple's 30-day example offers a security test, whether vulnerabilities can still be dealt with in time once other engines are allowed, and the migration cost Mozilla describes offers a competition test, whether users drop away when they have to switch apps.

item.title: Facial recognition gates at Hong Kong's Laguna City and the privacy commissioner's compliance check
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: On 13 November, Hong Kong's Office of the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data began a compliance check, on its own initiative, into the facial recognition access gates being installed at Laguna City, a private housing estate in Lam Tin, saying more than 8,000 households may be involved. The property management company said it would issue notices and hold sessions to introduce the system before launch, but its public responses do not say whether residents can keep using door cards or how long facial data will be kept. Readers outside Hong Kong are not affected.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 10 sources, including am730, Hong Kong Free Press, 點新聞

On 13 November, Hong Kong's Office of the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data (PCPD, the statutory body responsible for personal data protection) said it had begun a compliance check, on its own initiative, into the facial recognition access system at Laguna City. In a compliance check, the PCPD asks an organisation for information to see whether it is complying with the Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance. Laguna City is a private housing estate (the Hong Kong term for a large residential development) in Lam Tin, and according to the PCPD's statement more than 8,000 households may be involved. Laguna City residents are directly affected, other Hong Kong estates that bring in similar systems are bound by the same ordinance, and places outside Hong Kong are not affected.

Laguna City has four phases, and the property management company is installing facial recognition gates in phases 1, 2 and 4. A Sing Tao Headline reporter at the estate on 13 November saw installed gates still covered with paper. According to Dot Dot News, which relayed the company's response to the media, the gates are meant to make coming and going easier for residents and to improve management services, and before launch the company will hold tea gatherings and issue notices to introduce the system to residents. The company also said the personal data it collects will be handled in accordance with the ordinance, and Hong Kong Free Press (HKFP) reported that a Kwun Tong district councillor said on an RTHK programme that the system is due to go live in January.

HKFP also reported that the councillor had heard views both for and against, with some elderly residents finding the new system more convenient. Of the residents Sing Tao Headline interviewed, some said they would not use it because they worried about data leaks, and one found tapping a door card quicker and easier than facial recognition. Another planned to wait and see, and to try it once it is in use.

According to the PCPD's statement as quoted by HKFP, "facial images constitute sensitive personal data", and on that basis the PCPD asked the property management company for further information. According to the statement, the check is to make sure the company follows the ordinance and its data protection principles in collecting, holding, processing and using biometric data, in particular the requirements on data security. The data protection principles are the ordinance's basic rules on how personal data is collected, kept, used and protected. HKFP reported that the company told the media on 16 November that it would cooperate with the check.

Perspective

The property management company gave convenience as its reason for the gates, and some elderly residents see it the same way. The PCPD's Guidance on Collection and Use of Biometric Data, first published in 2015 and revised in 2020, lists facial images among physiological data, most of which cannot be changed. Among the consequences of wrongful disclosure of biometric data set out in the guidance are re-identification, impersonation and even discrimination. Its recommendations for reducing the risk include deriving templates (numerical values extracted from an image and used for matching) from the original images as soon as possible, safely discarding the originals, and storing templates in a form that is technically infeasible or difficult to convert back into images.

On our reading, alternatives, consent and how long data is kept are the questions that follow from the PCPD's earlier guidance and the gaps in the reports, while the focus of the check given in the statement is data security. The good practices in the biometric guidance include offering an alternative where practicable, and its example is a smartcard in place of fingerprint-based attendance at work. In the guidance's workplace example, the Privacy Commissioner will not interfere where people have another option and choose to register voluntarily, and if the same standard is applied here, whether door cards are kept bears on whether Laguna City residents' registration counts as voluntary. The president of the Hong Kong Institute of Housing told Sing Tao Headline that biometric authentication would become the norm, but that residential facial recognition must have residents' consent and should come with other ways of verifying identity for residents to choose from.

Before registering their faces, Laguna City residents can ask the property management company whether they can keep using door cards, how consent will be given at registration and how long the data will be kept, since none of these appears in the reports or the company's responses. After registering, residents can make a data access request, asking the organisation for a copy of the personal data it holds about them, and anyone who suspects their privacy has been infringed can complain to the PCPD (telephone 2827 2827). Our reading is that, in answering a data access request, an organisation supplies only the data it acknowledges holding, so residents would still find it hard to confirm whether facial templates count as data they can request, or whether backups are deleted too. The company has said it will issue notices and hold sessions to explain how the system works before launch, and residents can raise these questions there.

A compliance check is not a finding of a breach. According to the PCPD's explanation of the ordinance, when the Privacy Commissioner receives a complaint or has reasonable grounds to believe the ordinance has been contravened, the decision whether to investigate depends on the facts and evidence. If an investigation finds a contravention, the Privacy Commissioner can issue an enforcement notice directing the organisation to take remedial steps, and failing to comply with the notice is an offence. This site's 9 November article covered the plan to add facial recognition to the Hong Kong police's SmartView programme, a police CCTV network, whereas the Laguna City system is being brought in by the management company of a private estate.

In mainland China, under a 2021 judicial interpretation by the Supreme People's Court, where a property management company makes facial recognition the only way for owners or occupants to enter the area it manages, courts will support those who do not agree and ask for another reasonable means of verification. The Measures for the Security Management of Facial Recognition Technology Applications (人脸识别技术应用安全管理办法), in force since 1 June 2025, apply to facial recognition in general and do not address residential estates specifically. Under these measures, facial recognition may not be the only means of verification where other non-facial-recognition methods can achieve the same purpose or meet the same business requirements, and people who do not consent must be offered another reasonable and convenient way. Facial data may also be kept no longer than the shortest time needed for the purpose of processing.

According to a September 2026 report in Yangtse Evening Post, a court in Chongqing's Yuzhong District ordered a property company that had installed facial recognition gates at an estate's only entrance to delete an owner's facial and ID card data and to provide another reasonable way in, and neither side appealed. In Hong Kong, the alternative appears in the PCPD's guidance as a recommended good practice, to be offered as far as practicable.

Next, it is worth watching whether the PCPD publishes the result of the check, and how the property management company explains door-card alternatives and the retention period for facial data in its sessions and notices before launch.

item.title: Coding agent and developer tool records in Windows 11 diagnostic data
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Testing on a Windows 11 virtual machine, a researcher found that a system component records which coding agents and which kinds of developer tools have been run, and that the record is classed as optional diagnostic data and placed in the upload queue. Optional diagnostic data can be turned off in Settings. Microsoft's list of required diagnostic data separately includes a cohort event that reports whether a user is a developer, and Microsoft has not explained how it relates to these records.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 7 sources from xusheng.dev, Microsoft, Computerworld

Besides crash reports and hardware details, Windows 11 diagnostic data may also include which coding agents (AI tools that write and edit code for the user) and developer tools a person has run. In a post on his personal blog, a researcher used reverse engineering (taking a program apart to work out how it functions) and testing to show that one system component contains the executable names of coding agents such as codex.exe, claude.exe, copilot.exe and cursor.exe, and of developer tools such as python.exe and gcc.exe. The component matches the file name of a program when it runs, so readers can judge from the programs they normally run whether this concerns them. He tested the coding agent check on only one virtual machine of his own, and did not verify whether it is switched on for other computers.

According to the analysis he published on 16 November, a component called MissionControlAggregator reads the program launch records that Windows already keeps, and when a name matches, it sets a mark in a bitmap (a row of positions, each holding only yes or no). Coding agents are recorded one by one, while developer tools are recorded only by category, so GCC and Clang, for example, fall into the same one. In the researcher's reading, the component "appears to discard" the run times and interaction counts in the source records. He found no prompts or source code in the event, but considers that "collecting which agents and developer tools someone uses already has significant privacy implications."

Windows diagnostic data comes in two levels, required and optional, and according to Microsoft's support page, users can choose whether to send optional diagnostic data when they first set up Windows. The researcher also did a clean install of Windows 11 Home from the latest official image with the region set to the United States, and found the optional data switch already on before he changed any privacy setting. He used that installation only to check the switch's default, and did not check whether the coding agent records were enabled on it.

On the researcher's virtual machine, the coding agent check was already enabled, and he had not switched it on himself. With optional data allowed, he found a tool usage record in the Windows upload queue (where diagnostic data is held until it is sent), marked as optional data. His conclusion in the post is that the data is uploaded to Microsoft, but the evidence he lists stops at the record being queued, with no record of an actual outgoing connection.

Perspective

In Microsoft's guide for organizations on configuring diagnostic data, the contents of optional diagnostic data include "App activity, such as which programs are launched on a device, how long they run". The same guide states that the setting that sends no diagnostic data at all "is only available on Windows Server, Windows Enterprise, and Windows Education editions", so in our reading of the guide, Home and Pro users cannot turn off required data. Microsoft's published list of required diagnostic data includes a separate cohort event, Segments.Cohorts, described as one that "classifies users into Cohorts based on App usage", with the line "IsDeveloper is the only cohort being reported". It is a different event from the record the researcher captured, which is classed as optional, and Microsoft has neither published how a user is judged to be a developer nor explained whether the two are connected.

In mainland China, Microsoft released Windows 10 China Government Edition in 2017, developed with the Chinese technology and defence company China Electronics Technology Group Corp (CETC). In a Microsoft blog post quoted in a Computerworld column, the plan for the edition was to use Windows manageability features to remove features Chinese government employees do not need, such as OneDrive, "to manage all telemetry and updates", and to let the government use its own encryption algorithms. The researcher's tests ran on Windows 11 and did not cover this 2017 Windows 10 edition.

To see what diagnostic data your own computer sends, you can install the Diagnostic Data Viewer from the Microsoft Store, then go to Settings > Privacy & security > Diagnostics & feedback and switch on "Turn on the Diagnostic Data Viewer". Once it is on, Windows stores diagnostic data on the device until you turn it off, using up to 1 GB of the system drive by default, and according to the viewer's documentation, "We strongly recommend that you turn off data viewing when you're done". The instructions on the same page are to use the device as usual for a few days before coming back to look, and its wording on queued events is "Seeing an event doesn't necessarily mean it has been uploaded yet." As of 22 November, no one had publicly checked whether the tool usage records the researcher found appear in the viewer.

If you run developer tools or coding agents on Windows 11 and do not want that record to become part of your diagnostic data, you can turn off Send optional diagnostic data under Diagnostic data. The switch is on the same Settings page, and on a new installation you can also decline optional data during setup. Readers outside the United States can go straight to the Settings page to see the switch's current state.

The records the researcher found are marked optional, so in our reading of that label, they should no longer be queued for upload once the switch is off. According to Microsoft's support page, "Regardless of whether you choose to send Optional diagnostic data, your device will be just as secure and will operate normally." The researcher's post includes no comparison test with optional data turned off, and Microsoft has not published what the tool usage records are used for.

item.title: UK secrecy over the Apple technical capability notice and the Investigatory Powers Tribunal ruling
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: The Investigatory Powers Tribunal ruled on 19 November that the UK government had not shown that publicly confirming it gave Apple a technical capability notice would damage national security. Whether the notice is lawful has not been heard and its content has not been published. The parties indicate they are likely to agree arrangements aimed at a substantive hearing in the first half of 2027, and according to Apple's support page, users outside the UK could still turn on iCloud Advanced Data Protection as of 21 November.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 12 sources, including Investigatory Powers Tribunal, The Record, Privacy International

The Investigatory Powers Tribunal, a UK court that hears certain national security cases, published a judgment on 19 November finding that the government had not shown that publicly confirming it had given Apple a "technical capability notice" would damage national security. A technical capability notice is a government order requiring a company to maintain the ability to help with investigations, and the tribunal confirmed in the judgment that the government had given Apple one. The tribunal did not decide whether the notice is lawful, and it did not publish the notice's content.

On its support page about the UK, Apple writes that Advanced Data Protection (ADP, which lets only the user's own devices decrypt data such as iCloud backups and photos) "continues to be available everywhere else in the world." As of 21 November, new users in the UK still cannot turn ADP on, and those who already have it will need to turn it off themselves to keep using their iCloud account. Apple wrote that it would give them a period of time to do so, but MacRumors reported on 19 November that no deadline had yet been set, and we have not found a public statement from Apple on the ruling.

Since February 2025, media have reported that the UK government used the Investigatory Powers Act 2016 to require Apple to keep the ability to access user data in decrypted form. According to a timeline compiled by the advocacy group Privacy International, the UK reportedly withdrew one notice, and a second notice later reported by the Financial Times was believed to apply only to the UK. Apple and advocacy groups including Privacy International each challenged the notice, and the tribunal dealt with both challenges together.

The UK government follows a "neither confirm nor deny" policy on such notices, and argued before the tribunal that even confirming the notice existed would damage national security. The tribunal inferred that reports in The Times and the Financial Times citing government sources were based on briefings the government had authorised, and therefore found that official confirmation would not add materially to what malign actors already know. It agreed that making the notice's content and all of both sides' evidence public would damage national security, and left the question of which details can be disclosed until the parties have exchanged evidence. For the substantive hearing on whether the notice itself is lawful, the parties indicated that they are likely to agree arrangements aimed at the first half of 2027.

Perspective

In a statement after the ruling, quoted by The Record, a government spokesperson said Apple had been helping the police and intelligence agencies pursue criminals for several years, in accordance with the law, and that "This Technical Capability Notice simply requires that they maintain the ability to do so." Under iCloud's default standard data protection, data is encrypted but the keys are held in Apple's data centres. With ADP turned on, the keys for most data stay only on the user's trusted devices. Our reading of the government's statement is that maintaining that ability for accounts with ADP would require Apple to get hold of those keys again, while Apple wrote on its UK support page in September 2025 that "we have never built a backdoor or master key to any of our products or services and we never will."

In its challenge, Apple questions whether the powers in the Investigatory Powers Act can be used to regulate the security or privacy services a company offers, and whether the notice's interference with rights protected by the European Convention on Human Rights goes further than its aim requires. The spokesperson also said that the right to privacy is crucial but "should not come at the expense of the safety of the British public," and that decisions affecting the public's safety "must be made by democratically elected governments and independent judges, not in the boardrooms of technology companies."

The ruling does not change the current restriction for UK users; where ADP is offered, Apple's steps for iPhone and iPad go through Settings, your name and iCloud to Advanced Data Protection, where an account that has not enabled it will see Turn on Advanced Data Protection. Before turning it on you set up a recovery contact or recovery key. Once it is on, Apple does not have the keys needed to help with recovery, so if you lose access to your account you recover your data with one of those methods or your device passcode. With ADP on, iCloud Backup, iCloud Drive, Photos, Notes and other data move to end-to-end encryption, while Apple still holds the keys for iCloud Mail, Contacts and Calendars.

Apple's Traditional Chinese support pages for Taiwan and Hong Kong carry the same steps as the English page, consistent with the UK page's statement that ADP remains available everywhere else. In mainland China, iCloud is operated by GCBD (AIPO Cloud (Guizhou) Technology Co. Ltd), and according to Apple's privacy statement for customers in China, personal information on that service, including photos, documents and other iCloud data, is stored inside China. Whether accounts on GCBD-operated iCloud can turn on ADP is not stated on Apple's ADP support pages.

One of the questions for the substantive hearing is whether the powers in the Investigatory Powers Act can be used to regulate the security or privacy services a company offers its customers. In our reading, if they can, what follows is whether a company operating in the UK could still offer a design in which the keys stay only on users' devices, and whether the investigative effect the government wants could be achieved under such a design. The tribunal will also have to decide how much of the hearing can be held in public, weighing the British public's need to understand the scope of this power against the national security risks the government says disclosure would bring.

item.title: Native passkey integration in the Bitwarden desktop app for Windows 11 and macOS
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Relevant to people already using Bitwarden on Windows 11 or macOS. On 18 November Bitwarden announced that its desktop app can be set as the system's passkey provider, so passkeys created on a computer can be saved to the Bitwarden vault and synced with the account. Windows 11 requires the version installed from the Microsoft Store, and according to Privacy Guides' news brief, Linux users will not get the feature this time.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 11 sources, including Bitwarden, Privacy Guides, Microsoft

On 18 November Bitwarden announced that its desktop app can be set as the passkey provider (the program on a computer that stores passkeys and supplies them at sign-in) in Windows 11 and macOS. Passkeys replace passwords with the device's screen lock: the site stores only a public key, and the private key used to sign in stays on the device or in a password manager. With the desktop app set as the provider, the system dialog that appears when a website or desktop application creates a passkey lists Bitwarden as a place to save it. Windows 11 requires the version installed from the Microsoft Store, and according to Privacy Guides' news brief, Linux users will not get the feature this time.

Bitwarden began storing passkeys in its browser extension and mobile apps in early 2024. According to Privacy Guides' news brief of 19 November, the extension works for websites, but signing in to a desktop application might mean falling back on a phone or a hardware security key. Passkeys created on a computer might also end up in the default Windows or macOS credential manager rather than in Bitwarden.

A passkey created through the system dialog becomes a login item in the vault and can be managed from any Bitwarden app. If the vault already holds a login item with the same username, the passkey is added to that item automatically. If that item already contains a passkey, an overwrite warning appears first.

Perspective

The integration matters to people already using Bitwarden on Windows 11 or macOS, and those who do not use Bitwarden are unaffected. Once it is set up, passkeys created on the computer can be saved to Bitwarden and synced with the account to other devices, rather than staying in the system's default tool. In our reading of how the announcement describes syncing, the private keys follow the Bitwarden account, so the way that account is protected and recovered also bears on these passkeys. For anyone who later wants to move them to another password manager, the protocol for direct transfer is still a draft.

The dialogs for creating a passkey and signing in come from Windows 11 and macOS, while the private keys are kept in the Bitwarden vault. According to Microsoft's documentation, when Windows 11 is used with a third-party provider, the passkeys are protected and managed by that provider.

To move or back up passkeys by exporting to a file, only the .json format includes them, and Bitwarden recommends the encrypted option on its export page. Only a Password protected encrypted export can be imported into another Bitwarden account, while an Account restricted export can only go back into the account it came from. Passkeys created before Bitwarden 2024.3.1 carry a counter that increases with each use, and according to the export page, exports of passkeys that old should not be used as long-term backups.

On the same export page, direct transfer to another password manager is listed only for phones, with nothing on whether the desktop app can do it (which apps support it is covered in our 19 October piece on the passkey attestation debate). Direct transfer uses the FIDO Alliance's Credential Exchange Protocol (CXP), and as of 21 November the CXP listed on the FIDO Alliance's page was a working draft from October 2024.

To have new passkeys saved to the Bitwarden vault on Windows 11, use the desktop app from the Microsoft Store; the beta Bitwarden released in November 2025 was installed from GitHub instead. According to Microsoft's announcement, the capability arrived with the November 2025 security update. Next, under Passkey provider in the desktop app's settings, choose Manage in system settings and enable Bitwarden in the system dialog that follows; on macOS, the dialog asks whether to use AutoFill from Bitwarden. On its help page, Bitwarden recommends also turning off the passkey functions in the browser extension to prevent collisions between the two.

Bitwarden's cloud has two regions, the United States and the European Union, with none in mainland China, Hong Kong or Taiwan, and an account exists only in the region where it was created. In mainland China, GreatFire, a project that measures blocking by the Great Firewall, rated vault.bitwarden.com as not blocked, last tested on 15 November, and all five of its recent conclusive tests of that address connected normally. GreatFire rated bitwarden.com as sometimes accessible, with interference in one of its last four conclusive tests, the latest on 26 October. These tests check whether an address can be opened, which is not the same as whether the apps can sync, so in our reading they do not show whether the desktop app can sync passkeys with Bitwarden's servers from mainland China.

The passkey used to sign in to the Bitwarden account itself is not saved in the vault. Since the vault will not hold that key, people who sign in to Bitwarden with a passkey need to keep it somewhere else. Linux users, and Windows 11 users who would rather not switch to the Store version, can still store and use passkeys on websites through the browser extension, though that does not cover signing in to desktop applications.

item.title: OONI measurements of the Telegram blocks in Iraq and Jordan
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Iraq and Jordan announced blocks on Telegram on 16 November. In OONI Probe measurements, Telegram tests in both countries turned anomalous between 15 and 16 November (UTC) and were all still anomalous on 20 November. Both orders apply only to networks inside each country, and readers elsewhere are not affected by these blocks.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 14 sources, including net4people, OONI Explorer, OONI

A government that announces a block does not always state when it takes effect or which networks it covers, and people outside can check both against measurements taken on local networks. On 16 November Iraq's Communications and Media Commission announced a nationwide block on Telegram on the Prime Minister's instructions, and Jordan's Public Security Directorate announced a block the same day. In measurements from OONI Probe, open-source software from OONI (Open Observatory of Network Interference) for measuring network censorship, Telegram tests in both countries turned anomalous between 15 and 16 November (UTC) and were all still anomalous on the 20th. Both orders apply only to networks inside each country, and readers elsewhere are not affected by these blocks.

According to the commission's announcement, Telegram had not dealt with unlawful content on the platform or met its obligations under Iraqi law, and the operating company has 30 days to regularise its legal status. In the statement as Kurdistan24 reported it, there is no mention of which channels or posts the decision rested on, what steps must be taken within the 30 days, or what happens once they are up. According to Al Jazeera, Jordan's Public Security Directorate gave curbing illegal and extremist content as the reason for its block. Reuters reported that Telegram denies Iraq's accusations, and in the statement Telegram gave Reuters, its efforts to combat terrorism are described as going beyond what the law requires.

OONI Probe is run by users on their own networks, its results are published, and its dates are counted in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC). Before the block Iraq had 67 to 80 Telegram tests a day, with almost no anomalies. On the 16th, 33 of 72 tests were anomalous, and from the 17th every test was. According to a 19 November post compiling both countries' measurements on net4people, a public forum for discussing internet censorship, WhatsApp and Signal tests in Iraq stayed at their usual level that same week.

Jordan has far fewer measurements, between 1 and 8 a day before the block, none of them anomalous. On the 15th, 7 of 13 were anomalous, and from the 16th all of them were. Since OONI counts days in UTC and Jordan's local time is three hours ahead, the last three hours of 15 November UTC already fell on the 16th in Jordan. From these figures it is not possible to tell whether the anomalies began before the announcement.

Perspective

In OONI's Telegram test, Probe connects from the user's network to the servers the Telegram app uses, and also loads the web version at web.telegram.org. According to OONI's description of the test, Telegram is likely blocked when none of the app's servers can be reached or when the web version does not load properly. A measurement flagged as anomalous means its result matches one of these cases, and the reason the connection failed has to be worked out separately.

An AS (autonomous system) is a set of networks on the internet run by one operator or institution. Every measurement was anomalous on the 12 ASes in Iraq with data from 17 November onward, and on the 4 ASes in Jordan with data from the 16th onward. From these numbers it is not possible to tell what technique the blocks use or where in the network traffic is stopped. In general, the way traffic is intercepted affects whether other services are caught up as well.

The turning point is visible in both countries because normal daily measurements from before the blocks were already there to compare against. Measurements only cover networks where someone runs the test, and on networks like Jordan's, with single-digit tests a day, it is hard to pin down when the change happened. Anyone who wants to see the figures does not need to install anything, since OONI Explorer, OONI's public site for measurement results, can be searched by country and by the Telegram test.

Running Probe on your own network has a cost too. In OONI's FAQ, Probe is described as not a privacy tool, and anyone monitoring network activity (for example a government, an ISP or an employer) may be able to see that you are running it. On OONI's risks page, the potential risks of running Probe depend on the user's threat model (who they might face and what that party can do) and on the laws of the country they are in. On 20 November we covered choosing which tests to run in the app and not sending measurements, in the TLS Middlebox experiment in OONI Probe and a survey on data collection, and that even with those settings someone may still be able to see that Probe is running.

Between 22 August and 21 November, 2,231 of the 2,324 OONI Telegram tests in mainland China (about 96%) were flagged as anomalous, a label for signs of possible interference that on its own does not establish a block. Over the same period Taiwan had 177 anomalies in 11,530 tests (about 1.5%) and Hong Kong 15 in 2,485 (about 0.6%), so most tests in both places came back normal. GreatFire, which tests whether web addresses can be reached from mainland China, has recorded interference with telegram.org since July 2015 and found the site 100% blocked in its last test, on 18 October, though that figure is for the website rather than the app's message connections. Because about 96% of the tests in mainland China over that period were already anomalous, our reading is that a new block there would not show up as a jump in the anomaly share, the way the blocks in Iraq and Jordan did against days of normal results.

Readers outside Iraq and Jordan do not need to change any settings. According to Reuters, Iraq also blocked Telegram in 2023 and restored the service a week later, after a government statement that the company had responded to the security authorities' requirements. Once the two countries announce that the blocks are lifted, OONI Explorer is also where to check whether the Telegram tests return to normal.
