item.title: Payment and identity in SimpleX supporter badges
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: SimpleX Chat sells supporter badges that let buyers send larger files. By design, SimpleX cannot tell from a badge it is shown which purchase the badge came from, but card payments and badges grouped by expiry week still leave traces.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 10 sources, including SimpleX Chat, GitHub, IETF

SimpleX's announcement says that in other messaging apps a paid feature is attached to the account, so the operator knows who paid and what they do with the feature. Since September SimpleX Chat has sold supporter badges, which raise the file size limit from 1 GB to 2 GB (5 GB with a Legend badge) and keep files on servers for longer (7 days with a Supporter badge, 21 days with a Legend badge). The SimpleX network has no user accounts, so a badge is an anonymous credential that proves the holder paid without revealing who they are. As of 21 November, version 7.1 of the SimpleX Chat app includes the feature.

According to SimpleX's technical white paper, a badge is a BBS signature (a digital signature scheme still being standardised), issued by a badge service that SimpleX operates and stored on the user's own device. Each time the app shows the badge to a contact or presents it to a server, it generates a new zero-knowledge proof from it. A zero-knowledge proof works like proving you are over 18 without handing over your whole ID card, a technique we also covered in our piece on the EU age verification app. Contacts and server operators therefore receive only the badge type and expiry date, and cannot link two presentations to each other or trace either one back to the purchase.

SimpleX's announcement says credentials are issued one month at a time, and all badges expire on the same day of the week. A holder is therefore hidden among every supporter whose badge expires that week. According to the white paper, at each monthly renewal the app requests the new credential from the badge service and shows the new badge to contacts on different days, so that others find it harder to pick out a holder by timing.

Perspective

Privacy Pass, developed by the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF), takes a different approach: a user passes a check once in exchange for tokens, and can present them without revealing who they are. According to the white paper, these tokens are spent once presented and carry no expiry date or type. A badge has to be presented again and again, in every conversation and on every connection, so SimpleX chose BBS signatures, from which the app can keep generating new proofs.

The white paper says the badge service keeps the payment record of each purchase, and a card payment is linked to the purchase, as with any other service. Because badges expiring in the same week share one expiry date, server operators can group those supporters' connections together, and how many people a holder is hidden among depends on how many badges expire that week. A badge that has just been bought or redeemed from a code is shown right away, so for people who get a code in the badge service's own group, SimpleX can infer from when the new badge appears who redeemed it. When a Google Play subscription is moved to a new device with Restore purchases (the feature that moves the store's subscription to the current profile), SimpleX can link the two purchases, though not the profiles that hold them.

The Android version installed from Google Play takes payment inside the app, with a one-month plan and monthly or annual plans that renew automatically. The iOS version, versions installed from F-Droid or GitHub, and the desktop version open a purchase page in the browser, where paying by card, Bitcoin or Monero gives you a code to paste into the app's settings in exchange for a badge. The white paper says that people who want the payment itself to be private can pay with cryptocurrency instead. Badges bought on the web do not renew automatically and, as of 21 November, cannot be moved to a new device.

Mainland China and Taiwan are two examples. As of 21 November the China App Store had no listing for SimpleX Chat, and GreatFire (a project that measures blocking by the Great Firewall) found play.google.com blocked in mainland China as of 1 November. The Taiwan App Store did list the app. GreatFire also found simplex.chat, where the announcement sends badge buyers, blocked in mainland China in its latest test on 17 November, based on a single sample.

For those who pay by card, the payment record may also stay with the card issuer. A card issuer covered by mainland China's Anti-Money Laundering Law must keep customer identity data and transaction records for at least ten years (Article 34). In Taiwan, the Money Laundering Control Act requires covered institutions to keep customer identification records for at least five years after the relationship or an occasional transaction ends (Article 8).

A badge is attached to a single profile, and incognito profiles do not show it. Badges cannot be revoked, so if a device or backup is compromised, whoever obtains the badge data can use it until it expires. If several months were bought, the intruder can also request new credentials for the remaining months from the badge service.

item.title: The unlicensed-website conviction and closure order against Egypt's independent outlet Mada Masr
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: On 27 October, an Egyptian court fined the editor-in-chief of Mada Masr 3 million Egyptian pounds for running a news website without a licence, and ordered the site closed and its equipment confiscated. A hearing in a separate case against the editor-in-chief was set for 11 November, and as of 15 November we could not find its outcome. Readers outside Egypt do not need to change any settings.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 9 sources, including EFF, Al Jazeera, The National

According to Al Jazeera, the New Cairo Misdemeanour Court in Egypt convicted the editor-in-chief of the independent news site Mada Masr on 27 October of running a news website without a licence, and imposed the maximum fine allowed by law, 3 million Egyptian pounds. The court also ordered the site closed and the outlet's equipment confiscated. A hearing in a separate case against the editor-in-chief was set for 11 November, and as of 15 November we could not find its outcome. The ruling was made in Egypt, and readers elsewhere are not directly affected.

An article by the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) notes that Mada Masr has published only online since it was founded in 2013. EFF, Reporters Without Borders (RSF) and The National all report that the site has been blocked inside Egypt since 2017. According to a report at the time by the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), the Supreme Council for Media Regulation (SCMR), which handles media licences, announced a further six-month block of the site in October 2023.

According to The National, the Supreme State Security Prosecution questioned the editor-in-chief for more than six hours on 21 October about a report Mada Masr had published, and she was released on bail of 100,000 Egyptian pounds. The next day prosecutors sent her to trial on the licensing charge, and EFF writes that the proceedings took a single hearing. Al Jazeera reports that she was taken into custody after the ruling and released several hours later once Mada Masr paid the fine in full, while EFF's article and a joint statement by several organisations put her detention at seven hours. The National also counts this as the sixth case against Mada Masr or its journalists in six years, and EFF's article cites CPJ's count of at least 25 journalists imprisoned in Egypt.

According to a Mada Masr editorial quoted by Al Jazeera, the court refused the defence's requests to examine the case file, present evidence and call witnesses. The editorial also says the judge appointed a separate lawyer to defend the editor-in-chief, although all eight of her lawyers were present and she objected. That joint statement, issued on 28 October by the Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy (TIMEP) and other organisations, says Mada Masr's legal team plans to appeal. Al Jazeera also reports that the head of the Egyptian Journalists' Syndicate said the union would take legal action.

EFF's article of 2 November describes the 11 November hearing as the second trial in two weeks, on a charge of spreading false news. Al Jazeera and the joint statement describe it as a hearing to review a 2024 conviction in absentia on charges of publishing false news and running an unlicensed website. According to both, the editor-in-chief learned while being processed for release on 27 October that she had been sentenced in absentia to one year in prison in 2024. Al Jazeera, citing Mada Masr, reports that her lawyers challenged that ruling and the court set a hearing for 11 November, which Al Jazeera calls a retrial.

Perspective

Al Jazeera reported no immediate official comment on the 27 October ruling. As of 15 November we could not find any public statement on the ruling from the Egyptian government or the SCMR, and the only accounts available come from Mada Masr and advocacy groups.

According to Al Jazeera, the ruling rests on Egypt's 2018 media law, which sets a fine of 1 million to 3 million Egyptian pounds for running an unlicensed website, along with closure of the site and confiscation of equipment. The same report says an administrative court in 2023 upheld the SCMR's rejection of Mada Masr's licence application, on the grounds that there was no proof the outlet's trademark had been registered. Mada Masr's account is that its applications in 2018 and 2020 went unanswered and that it learned of the rejection only from prosecutors during another case in 2022, and its lawyer said he had submitted a trademark registration certificate.

EFF's article argues that requiring news organisations to obtain government authorisation to operate creates a mechanism for restricting who gets to publish. The joint statement from TIMEP and other organisations, whose signatories include Access Now, Amnesty International and ARTICLE 19, calls on the government to grant licences to independent outlets without discrimination and to stop using the licensing provisions of the media law to criminalise journalism. A new application Mada Masr filed in June 2023 was still pending when Al Jazeera reported on the ruling.

According to CPJ's report, the SCMR gave two reasons for the 2023 block, "practicing media activities without a license" and "publishing false news without checking its sources," and also referred that case to the prosecutor general. We could not find any public information on the basis of the charges in the 2024 conviction in absentia. On false news charges, EFF argues that governments should not decide which reporting may be published, especially when the reporting concerns their own conduct.

OONI (Open Observatory of Network Interference) publishes censorship measurements run by volunteers in many countries. Each time a probe tests a website, a control connection is also made from an uncensored network, and the measurement is flagged as an anomaly when the two results differ. OONI's public API shows 33 measurements of madamasr.com recorded as Egypt between 16 October and 15 November (we queried on 15 November), of which 22 were flagged as anomalies, 2 failed and none was confirmed as blocked. Of the remaining 9 measurements with no anomaly, 6 came from Cloudflare's network rather than an ordinary Egyptian internet provider, so they do not reflect what typical users see.

In the two anomalous measurements we sampled, the Domain Name System (DNS) lookup matched the control, and the anomaly was an HTTP connection reset, meaning the connection was cut off after it was set up and the page did not load. Anomalous measurements have appeared every month since November 2025, with only 3 or 4 a month from July to September and 15 in October. The number of measurements is small and OONI only flags them as anomalies, so these data alone cannot show whether the site is still blocked in Egypt. Nor do the measurements show whether or how the 27 October closure order has been carried out (our inference).

Readers outside Egypt do not need to change any settings. Anyone who wants to check whether a site can be reached in different places can look up its public measurement records by URL in OONI Explorer. Developments worth following are the outcome of the 11 November hearing, the appeal against the 27 October ruling, and whether the site is actually closed under the order.

In mainland China, Article 5 of the Provisions on the Administration of Internet News Information Services, in force since June 2017, requires a permit to provide internet news information services through websites, apps, social media accounts and other channels. Under Article 22, providing such services without a permit leads to an order to stop and a fine of 10,000 to 30,000 yuan, according to the text published on the Cyberspace Administration of China's website (checked on 15 November). In Myanmar, CPJ reported, citing news reports, that the state broadcaster MRTV announced on 8 March 2021 that the military government had revoked the operating licences of five independent outlets, which were general operating licences rather than a permit specific to online news. CPJ also cited The New York Times as reporting that losing the licences could make reporting illegal for the five.

When comparing how different places regulate online media, one can ask whether licence decisions have a deadline, whether rejections come with reasons, whether applicants have a remedy, and whether operating without a licence is punished with a fine or with closure. Other questions are whether the authorities have published what the licensing regime and the false news offences are meant to achieve, and how much of that has been achieved since they took effect.

item.title: CSWP 50, NIST's cybersecurity guide for one-person businesses
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: On 2 November NIST published CSWP 50, a guide for one-person businesses with no employees that sets out actions such as multi-factor authentication, backups, updates and recognising phishing, written for readers with no security background. The guide is free to download, and as of 15 November we found only an English version. It is written for a US audience, though freelancers and self-employed people elsewhere can draw on its practices.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 7 sources, including NIST, Administration for Cyber Security, Ministry of Digital Affairs (Taiwan), Information-technology Promotion Agency, Japan (IPA)

On 2 November the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) published CSWP 50, Small Business Cybersecurity: Non-Employer Firms, a guide for one-person businesses with no employees, where the owner is the only paid worker. According to the press release, the guide is written in lay language and assumes no prior cybersecurity knowledge. It is final and free to download, and as of 15 November we found only an English version.

According to the guide, it was developed for a US audience, though many small businesses engage in international commerce or collaborations and the content can be adapted to support that work. Freelancers and self-employed people outside the US can draw on its practices. We infer that the US laws and support programmes it mentions do not apply elsewhere, and readers will need to substitute local equivalents.

According to the press release, more than 28 million small businesses in the US are one-person businesses. In the guide's abstract, the audience is "non-employer" firms as defined by the US Small Business Administration (SBA), meaning businesses with no employees other than the owner, and the guide may also be useful to businesses with very few employees or minimal IT infrastructure. The section on audience covers sole proprietors, freelancers, single-member limited liability companies (LLCs), independent contractors and gig economy workers, and counts the consultants that many small businesses rely on as another key audience.

According to the press release, the earlier guide, NISTIR 7621, was aimed at small businesses of varying sizes, while the revised CSWP 50 concentrates on protecting digital systems from malicious attack. The guide is based on version 2.0 of the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF 2.0, the structure NIST uses to organise an organisation's cybersecurity work) and is much more detailed than the CSF quick-start guide for small businesses. In the middle section, as the press release describes it, are actions a one-person business can take, each with the reason for it, how to get started and options once the business grows. The last part has a worksheet for inventorying assets, a table for tracking completed actions, and three hypothetical cases (a lawyer, an artisan and a business consultant), which are in a separate appendix file.

The guide's introduction has a list of nine actions that can significantly reduce risk. The first is to turn on phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication (MFA, which asks for a second form of verification besides the password at login) on accounts that offer it, especially email, banking, password managers and critical cloud services. Following NIST's guidance, passwords should be at least 15 characters long, a password manager is worth considering, and where possible passkeys can be used instead (a passkey is a login credential unlocked with a fingerprint, face or PIN on the device, with no username and password to type).

The other actions are learning to recognise phishing and ransomware, using a standard user account for routine work, inventorying important assets and the services the business depends on, setting up and testing backups, and keeping all devices and apps updated. The last two are listing the internal and external contacts to notify when an incident happens and keeping a printed copy, and listing the laws, regulations and contractual requirements that relate to cybersecurity. The ransomware section advises securing and isolating backups of important data, and the backup item in Chapter 3 also suggests considering at least one copy on a medium that is not connected to the device, such as an external hard drive or the cloud.

The guide's advice is to avoid mixing personal and business assets where possible, keeping personal devices separate from business devices. Where a device has to be shared with family members, each person should have their own account, and family members' accounts should not have access to sensitive business data. Another point in the guide is that home, cafés and co-working spaces each carry different physical threats, and that devices should have location tracking and remote wipe turned on.

For requests to change bank account details, amend an invoice, make an urgent payment or buy gift cards, the guide advises confirming through known or public contact details rather than replying to the message itself. The phishing section also mentions that AI products and services can now be used to craft more convincing phishing messages, and the guide calls them "Super Intelligence" (SI).

A footnote in the guide explains that SI follows a US executive order of 29 September, which directed executive agencies to change their usage from "artificial intelligence" to "super intelligence". A separate section on AI tools recommends taking stock of the AI tools in use and the AI features built into other software. Before entering sensitive information, users should check the settings for data retention, use for training and access permissions, and AI-generated content should be reviewed before it is used.

Perspective

In the guide's explanation of MFA, turning it on for every account that offers it is one of the most important steps for protecting a business. The same explanation mentions that some forms of MFA are susceptible to phishing, and gives passkeys as the phishing-resistant example. In common phishing techniques, a one-time code from a text message or an authenticator app can be captured by a fake site and passed on. A passkey is bound to the site where it was registered, so a fake site has difficulty obtaining a usable credential.

The press release quotes one of the authors as saying that many of the actions can be carried out on one's own with limited technical knowledge or minimal financial investment. The guide mentions only in passing that a password manager is a relatively inexpensive approach, and it does not estimate the cost of each action. Instead of doing the work themselves, owners can also hand it to a consultant or an outside provider, and the guide cautions that outsourcing does not transfer the responsibility for protecting systems and data.

Readers who want a Chinese-language counterpart can turn to the guidelines on basic cybersecurity protection for small and medium-sized enterprises, or SMEs (中小企業基本資安防護指引) from Taiwan's Administration for Cyber Security, part of the Ministry of Digital Affairs, which carries a cover date of March 2026. The 11-page PDF covers three areas (account management, device and data management, and security awareness) and comes with a self-assessment checklist. It is written for SMEs, with nothing separate for one-person businesses. Comparing the two documents, we found that the checklist's items on passwords of at least 15 characters, changing default passwords on connected devices, backups, automatic updates and an asset inventory all overlap with NIST's recommendations.

We, a community based in Taiwan, also looked at guidance from public bodies in Japan, Singapore and Hong Kong (checked on 15 November), and like Taiwan's, each is aimed at SMEs in general rather than at one-person businesses. Japan's Information-technology Promotion Agency (IPA) published version 4.0 of its guidelines on information security measures for SMEs (中小企業の情報セキュリティ対策ガイドライン) on 27 March 2026, a 70-page main volume in Japanese, while the English edition linked from that page is version 3.1. The Cyber Security Agency of Singapore (CSA) offers toolkits for enterprise leaders and SME owners, aimed at businesses that may not have dedicated IT staff and listed on its page as English PDFs. In Hong Kong, the Hong Kong Computer Emergency Response Team Coordination Centre (HKCERT) released Seven Habits of Cyber Security for SMEs, which includes a self-assessment checklist, in September 2018, and an Incident Response Guideline for SMEs, also written for non-technical readers, in July 2022.

People with no employees who look after all their own accounts and devices can start by checking their situation against the nine actions in the introduction, one at a time. The guide is a free 33-page English PDF on the NIST website, with the inventory worksheets and the three cases in a separate .xlsx file. The press release also quotes one of the authors as saying that the guide will not address all the needs of every one-person business. According to Chapter 3, the actions in its tables are not intended as a checklist or compliance criteria, and privacy is mostly outside the guide's scope apart from a few basic steps.

item.title: Weekly brief, 2026 week 47
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Eight stories from 2 to 14 November: Humble Bundle dropping two-factor authentication in its redesign, Outlook.com wrongly rejecting mail from domains without a DMARC record, Tails 7.17 and two minor Tor Browser releases, Mullvad Browser 16.0, a bypass of ChatGPT's Lockdown Mode, Zcash's NU7 upgrade, Hong Kong customs confiscating books from Taiwan ordered by a prisoner support group, and a German ministerial draft narrowing freedom of information.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 22 sources, including PC Gamer, Privacy Guides, Notebookcheck

There was no issue in weeks 45 and 46, so this one collects eight stories from both weeks, two of them follow-ups to earlier articles. The reports and announcements are dated between 2 and 14 November.

Two-factor authentication after Humble Bundle's redesign

According to a PC Gamer report on 12 November, the newly launched website of Humble Bundle, a digital game store, has no two-factor authentication (2FA, a one-time code entered at login in addition to the password). Users cannot add it, and accounts that had it set up can log in with just an email address and password. A Privacy Guides article on 13 November added that changing the password no longer requires verification, and changing the email address no longer sends a confirmation to the original inbox. The PC Gamer writer recommended removing any payment details saved in the account, and noted that some users reported difficulty doing so.

According to a Notebookcheck report on 14 November, some users say two-factor authentication is working again. Notebookcheck also wrote that there has been no official confirmation that it has been restored for everyone. As of 15 November, we had found no official statement from Humble Bundle.

Mistaken DMARC rejections at Outlook.com

According to a blog post by the email provider MailRoute, from 5 November Microsoft's consumer mail services, including Outlook.com, Hotmail and Live, rejected some mail from domains without a DMARC record. DMARC is a sender authentication policy that a domain publishes in DNS, and together with SPF and DKIM (two other sender authentication mechanisms) it lets the receiving side confirm that a message really comes from that domain. Most of the affected domains already had SPF set up, and many also had DKIM. On 6 November MailRoute initially read the rejections as Microsoft requiring every sender to set up DMARC, and withdrew that reading in an update on 10 November.

The Register cited Microsoft's incident report EX1545193, which attributes the problem to a spam rule update that wrongly flagged and blocked mail. According to Microsoft's account as relayed by MailRoute, the update has been rolled back and the rejections ended at 11:02 UTC (19:02 Taipei time) on 9 November. Expert Insights quoted a Microsoft spokesperson as saying senders do not need to change their settings.

Under Microsoft's 2025 announcement, only domains sending more than 5,000 messages a day to Outlook.com have had to pass SPF, DKIM and DMARC since 5 May 2025. MailRoute warned that Outlook.com does not retry rejected mail, so important messages bounced between 5 and 9 November need to be sent again.

Tails 7.17 and Tor Browser 16.0.1 and 16.0.2

Our 5 November article, "Tor Browser 16.0 and Tails 7.16", covered the previous versions of both. According to the Tor Project's announcement on 10 November, Tor Browser 16.0.1 includes important security updates to Firefox, rebasing onto Firefox 153.7.0esr and bringing in security fixes from Firefox 160. Tor itself is updated to 0.4.9.16.

The same day brought an Android-only 16.0.2, which fixes a breakage on Android caused by the zlib (compression library) update in 16.0.1. Neither announcement lists CVE numbers for individual vulnerabilities.

According to Tails' announcement on 11 November, version 7.17 updates Tor Browser to 16.0.1, Tor to 0.4.9.16 and the Linux kernel to 6.12.116. Tails 7.0 or later can upgrade to 7.17 automatically. Reinstalling instead erases the Persistent Storage on the USB stick.

Mullvad Browser 16.0

According to release notes published on 6 November by Mullvad, a VPN provider, Mullvad Browser 16.0 is the first version based on Firefox ESR 153, with a settings page redesigned along the lines of Firefox's June overhaul. There is now also a native build for Linux computers with 64-bit ARM processors, such as the Raspberry Pi. A new generic window title option replaces every window title with "Mullvad Browser" when turned on, because other programs on the computer and the operating system can read window titles without special permissions.

The release notes say the option is off by default because there was not enough time in this release cycle to evaluate side effects, and turning it on may make the browser harder to use for people who rely on accessibility tools such as screen readers. Our 5 November article covered the same option in Tor Browser 16.0.

The encrypted DNS settings are reduced to two choices, using DoH (DNS over HTTPS, which encrypts DNS queries before sending them) or using the operating system's DNS, which Mullvad recommends with a VPN. Our 30 September article, "An Android VPN leak and the end of Mullvad's public encrypted DNS", covered Mullvad shutting down its public encrypted DNS service. According to these release notes, browsers that used that service will be moved automatically to Quad9, a non-profit public DNS service. Customized DoH settings will not be changed, and anyone who manually chose a variant of Mullvad's encrypted DNS (base or family, for example) should switch back to the default option.

The ChatGPT Lockdown Mode bypass

According to an article on 5 November by Check Point Research, the research arm of the security company Check Point, Lockdown Mode is an optional advanced security setting for logged-in ChatGPT users. Turning it on restricts live web access, stops images from the internet from loading and disables file downloads, among other things, cutting down the ways data can leave a conversation. The researchers found that the HTML preview OpenAI added to code blocks in February could open pop-up windows free of the sandbox (the mechanism that isolates web content and limits what it can do), bypassing Lockdown Mode's protections.

In ChatGPT Classic, the desktop app built on the Electron framework, the attack needs no action from the user. The researchers demonstrated a malicious custom GPT (a version of ChatGPT that users can build and share) quietly sending messages from the conversation to an attacker's server. In the browser, the phishing and malware delivery scenarios require the user to click a preview the attacker has designed.

According to Check Point's account, OpenAI told the researchers on 18 September that it had removed the pop-up permissions from the preview sandbox. The researchers retested and confirmed that the technique no longer works. The article does not ask users to update any software. As of 15 November, we had found no public statement from OpenAI about the vulnerability.

Zcash's NU7 upgrade

According to a ForkLog report on 6 November, the mainnet of Zcash, a privacy-focused cryptocurrency, activated the NU7 network upgrade that day at block height 3,543,405, cutting the target block interval from 75 seconds to 25. As the report's example puts it, an exchange that requires three confirmations would credit deposits in about 75 seconds instead of 225. Miners' share of transaction fees drops to 40%, and the other 60% is taken out of circulation for now, to be paid out gradually as extra block rewards from around February 2031.

ForkLog also wrote that NU7 disables v4 transactions, the only format that can withdraw from Sprout, the first-generation shielded transaction system. About 12,224 ZEC left in Sprout can therefore no longer be spent, and NU7 comes with no recovery mechanism. The release notes for Zebra 7.0.0, the node software the Zcash Foundation published on 22 October, warn that mainnet nodes must upgrade before the activation height to stay on the consensus chain. ZIP 259, the NU7 deployment specification, also states that nodes that have not upgraded will remain on the old chain.

Books from Taiwan seized by Hong Kong customs, and a national security arrest

According to a Hong Kong Free Press report on 4 November, a group that supports people in prison announced on social media on 2 November that two boxes of books it had ordered from Taiwan were down to half a box when they reached its partner retail outlet on 20 October. More than 60 books were missing.

According to the same report, the customs notice to the logistics firm cited new rules added in March to the Beijing-imposed national security law for Hong Kong, which allow customs officers to seize items suspected of having seditious intention even when no one has been arrested. The group's statement said the seized books were rational discussions of current affairs and personal experiences, with no connection to seditious intention. Hong Kong Free Press described this as the first known case of books being confiscated without any accompanying arrest.

According to a police statement relayed by The Standard, the National Security Department of the Hong Kong Police Force arrested a man in Mong Kok on the morning of 5 November on suspicion of importing publications with seditious intention under the Safeguarding National Security Ordinance, which Hong Kong enacted locally. The offence carries a maximum sentence of seven years in prison. Hong Kong Free Press reported on 6 November that the arrested man is understood to be a project manager at the same group.

According to the South China Morning Post, a customs spokesperson said the department would not comment on individual cases, and would detain items suspected of having seditious intention in accordance with the law and refer cases to the National Security Department where appropriate. According to the same report, the man was still being held for questioning as of the evening of 5 November. As of 15 November, we had found no reports of charges or bail.

A German ministerial draft narrowing the Freedom of Information Act

Germany's federal Freedom of Information Act (IFG) lets anyone request access to official information held by federal authorities. According to a netzpolitik.org report on 5 November, the freedom of information platform FragDenStaat published a ministerial draft (Referentenentwurf, a version drawn up by a ministry and not yet sent to the cabinet) of the Federal Ministry of the Interior's Transparency Adjustment Act (Transparenz-Anpassungsgesetz). The draft would exclude a number of policy areas classed as "critical infrastructure" from the scope of the Act. In a report on 10 November, netzpolitik.org cited FragDenStaat as listing the excluded areas as energy, transport, finance, health, water, food, information technology and telecommunications.

According to an article by Human Rights Watch (HRW) on 11 November, the government put forward the draft on 30 September, and it leaked on 5 November. An earlier attempt at narrowing the Act in June failed in the face of opposition from civil society and from the Social Democrats (SPD), a member of the governing coalition.

netzpolitik.org's 10 November report also gathered the critics' views. The federal managing director of the journalists' union dju said that shutting journalists out from the start is a direct attack on press freedom. A head of division at the office of the Federal Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information wrote in a statement that the draft's exclusions go too far and are legally questionable.

HRW argued in its article that the current law already rules out disclosing information that could endanger public security, making the draft's restrictions unnecessary. As of 15 November, we had found no response from the Federal Ministry of the Interior to these criticisms, and no information on which stage of the process the draft has reached.

item.title: The Bureau of Consular Affairs website breach and 72,702 leaked passport photo files
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Taiwan's Bureau of Consular Affairs, part of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, found on 4 November that some of its websites had been broken into. Some passport photos uploaded between 3 September and 2 November through online appointments, travel agency bulk applications and conditional online passport renewal were leaked, 72,702 files in all. Applications made over the counter or through the one-stop service at household registration offices are not included. According to the bureau's announcement and Q&A, passports remain valid, and people confirmed to be within the scope can get a free replacement until 14 May 2027 (checked on 15 November). Some letters of authorisation verified by Taiwan's representative office in New York and some ABTC application data were also leaked, and ABTC applicants can ask to change their photo until 31 December.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 16 sources, including 外交部領事事務局, iThome, 風傳媒

Taiwan's Bureau of Consular Affairs (BOCA), part of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, announced on 9 November that some of its websites had been broken into, and in an update on 12 November confirmed that three kinds of data had been taken without authorisation. The largest set is passport photos: some of the photos people uploaded between 3 September and 2 November through individual online appointments, bulk applications filed by travel agencies and the conditional online passport renewal service, 72,702 files in all. Applications made over the counter or through the one-stop service at household registration offices are not included, and the official Q&A notes that not everyone who applied through those three channels in that period is affected. According to the bureau, passports already issued remain valid, and people confirmed to be within the scope can apply for a free replacement until 14 May 2027.

According to BOCA's announcement, it began finding signs on the afternoon of 4 November that some of its websites had been intruded upon, and it immediately isolated the servers involved, preserved evidence and reported the incident to the cybersecurity authority. The websites came back online after the code was repaired and security tested. Citing a digital forensics report, the official Q&A says no leak of other personal data, such as names, dates of birth, national ID numbers or passport numbers, has been found. As of 15 November, official documents did not state the cause of the intrusion or name the contractor involved.

The second set is scanned letters of authorisation verified by Taiwan's representative office in New York between 26 October 2011 and 6 November 2026, 26,072 files in all. According to the Q&A on these letters, they were verified for overseas Taiwanese living in New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Connecticut who authorised relatives or friends in Taiwan to handle matters on their behalf. Cases handled in Taiwan or at other overseas missions are not included. Original letters still within their authorisation period remain valid and do not need to be redone.

The third set is application data for the APEC Business Travel Card (ABTC), a business travel card that applicants obtain through BOCA. According to the ABTC Q&A, the application data includes the application category (such as manufacturing, wholesale or finance), job title and nominating agency. The announcement says what was taken is part of the data submitted through the online application form between 1 September and 10 November, covering 774 applications. Besides those three fields, the leaked data includes the applicant's photo, application number, sex and place of birth, but not names, passport numbers or contact details.

The announcement also says that if the contractor is found to have failed to meet the security obligations in its contract, the bureau will pursue its liability and seek compensation under the law. BOCA will also compile evidence and refer the intrusion to the judicial authorities for investigation.

Perspective

According to the official Q&A updated on 13 November, a passport photo can identify a person, so it is personal data protected under Taiwan's Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA). No specific misuse has been confirmed as resulting from the incident. Anyone who finds their photo being misused or used in a scam should keep the evidence and report it to the police. In the Q&A's words, as long as a person's facial features have not changed, there should be no need to apply for a new passport because of the incident.

Under Taiwan's Cyber Security Management Act as amended in September 2025, a government agency that becomes aware of a cybersecurity incident must report it to the competent authority and to its superior or supervising agency, and then submit a report on its investigation, handling and improvements. The same Act requires government agencies that outsource the operation of information systems to supervise the contractor's security management and to set out liability for breach of contract in a written agreement.

Under the current PDPA, an agency that violates the Act, resulting in personal data being stolen or leaked, must notify the people concerned by appropriate means after the facts are established, and official documents take no position on whether BOCA violated the Act. Amendments promulgated in November 2025 but not yet in force would instead require notification as soon as an agency becomes aware that personal data has leaked, and as of 15 November the Laws & Regulations Database still listed their effective date as undetermined. The Q&A on the letters of authorisation says the bureau has reported the incident to the PDPA's competent authority as required by law. As of 15 November, the only public channels were the announcement and a hotline for checking whether a photo was leaked (details below), and official documents did not say whether people whose photos fall within the scope would be notified individually.

Rules elsewhere in Asia offer a comparison, though none of them apply to this Taiwanese incident: as of 9 October 2026, data users in Hong Kong had no statutory duty to report a personal data breach to the Office of the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data (PCPD), whose June 2023 guidance recommends notifying the office and the affected people as soon as practicable. Making breach notification mandatory was among the amendment proposals the government listed in January 2025, and government papers to the Legislative Council in July 2026 still described amending the privacy ordinance as under study. In Singapore, the Personal Data Protection Commission (PDPC) states on its page about the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 that the Act generally does not apply to public agencies in relation to collecting, using or disclosing personal data (as of 15 November), so its breach notification duties, such as notifying the PDPC within three calendar days of assessing a breach as notifiable (as of 9 October 2026), generally would not cover a breach at a ministry itself (our inference). Under the same Act, a data intermediary processing personal data on behalf of a public agency must notify that agency of a breach without undue delay (as of 9 October 2026).

In mainland China, Article 57 of the Personal Information Protection Law requires any personal information handler, public or private, to take remedial measures immediately when a leak occurs or may occur, and to notify the authorities responsible for personal information protection and the affected individuals, without setting a number of days. Separately, the national cybersecurity incident reporting measures issued by the Cyberspace Administration of China, in force since 1 November 2025, require departments of central and state organs and their directly affiliated units to report to their own department's cyber affairs office within two hours, against four hours to the provincial cyberspace office for most other network operators. That deadline applies only to incidents graded "relatively major" or above, and the grading guide attached to the measures usually puts a leak of personal information on one million people or more in that grade (a general clause on large volumes sets no figure). The measures cover cybersecurity incidents rather than personal information leaks as such (as of 9 October 2026).

People who applied through online appointments, travel agency bulk applications or conditional online renewal between 3 September and 2 November can check whether their photo was leaked by calling a hotline set up by a contractor BOCA commissioned, (02) 8979-3100, from 09:00 to 12:00 and 13:30 to 18:00 on weekdays. Other questions about the incident and replacements can go to the bureau's passport issuance division at (02) 2343-2807 or (02) 2343-2808, or by email to boca4006@boca.gov.tw. Grantors and grantees of letters of authorisation with questions can call the document authentication enquiry line at +886-2-2343-2913 or contact the New York office at +1-212-486-0088.

The free replacement is open only to people confirmed to be within the scope of the leak whose passports have been issued and are still valid, and applications are in principle accepted for six months after the measure was announced on 13 November. Applicants go in person to BOCA or one of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs' four regional offices with proof of identity, a photo and the old passport, and someone applying on another person's behalf needs a letter of authorisation. The new passport is issued once free of charge with a full validity period, the old one is surrendered, and all new passports are sent by post. Whether to replace is left to each person's own judgement.

The official Q&A reminds applicants that a new passport comes with a new passport number and new issue and expiry dates, so anyone who has already used the old passport for visas, tickets or other travel arrangements should check whether they are affected. A replacement brings a new photo, number and validity period, but the leaked photos still show the holder's face, and replacing the passport cannot retrieve them (our inference).

ABTC applicants worried about their photo can ask to change it before 31 December by sending a new photo to abtc1@boca.gov.tw or calling (02) 2343-2975. The email subject should give the 12-digit application number and the words "更換照片" ("change photo"). For applications still under review, BOCA replaces the photo in its system. Cardholders can get a free replacement card, which takes 10 working days, and the old card is cancelled and cannot be used in the meantime.

The ABTC Q&A advises not giving personal data or clicking links when unknown calls, emails or messages ask for them, and verifying instead through the channels listed on BOCA's official website or by calling the 165 anti-fraud hotline. According to a Storm Media report of 12 November, BOCA had previously received reports of social engineering emails (messages that impersonate an official body to lure recipients into clicking a link or filling in data) sent in the name of confirmation emails from its "passport photo upload system". The report advised calling the official hotline directly on receiving an email or text message claiming to be from BOCA that asks you to click a link to "confirm your photo" or "fill in missing data". We did not find this warning in the official passport photo Q&A updated on 13 November.

People who did not apply for a passport through those three channels in that period, did not have a letter of authorisation verified at the New York office and did not use the ABTC online form have nothing to do because of this incident (the anti-scam advice still applies). Next to watch are the full forensic findings, the inquiry into the contractor's liability and the criminal referral, and whether BOCA notifies people whose photos fall within the scope individually.

item.title: The FBMD Identifier in Facebook Photos and Its Removal in Brave's Desktop Browser
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: From version 1.98, Brave's desktop browser automatically strips the FBMD identifier that Meta adds to Facebook photos whenever an image is saved or uploaded. Location, device and capture time are not removed, and as of 15 November the Android and iOS versions do not have the feature.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 10 sources, including Brave, GitHub, IPTC

Brave announced on 12 November that, from version 1.98, its desktop browser automatically removes the FBMD identifier that Meta adds to Facebook photos whenever an image is saved or uploaded. People using Brave on desktop get the protection once they update. As of 15 November the Android and iOS versions do not have it, and the announcement describes them only as planned. A photo's location, device model and capture time are outside the scope of this change.

According to Brave's announcement, Meta stores the identifier in photo metadata (data attached to the file that is not normally visible) defined by the International Press Telecommunications Council (IPTC). The IPTC sets standards for the news industry, and photographers and publishers use its formats to embed captions, author names and copyright information in images.

When the IPTC tested how Facebook handles uploaded photos, it found that Facebook deleted most of the existing metadata and added a long string beginning with FBMD to the "Special Instructions" field. When someone else downloaded the same photo and uploaded it again, the value stayed the same. Brave repeated the test in July and found the identifier still there.

The announcement describes a hypothetical person who runs an Instagram account under a different name, kept apart from the real-name Facebook account that family and colleagues know. They use a separate email alias for each account, and maybe a VPN to hide their IP address. If they download an image a friend posted on Facebook urging people to vote and share it on their Instagram, the identifier travels with the file, and Meta could use it to link the Instagram account to the friend's post and the real-name network around it. Once that link exists, Meta might suggest the Instagram account to people who know them on Facebook, and the link could also leak or be handed over in response to a legal request.

Brave's announcement notes that Meta has not disclosed what the identifier is for or why it is placed in image metadata. The announcement also acknowledges that Meta may not use it for tracking, and states that without public information Brave weighs every possibility and its privacy implications. As of 15 November we could find no explanation from Meta about the identifier or about Brave's announcement, and no retest other than Brave's since the IPTC's 2019 round.

When an image is saved, Brave removes the identifier before the download finishes, so it does not come along if the file is later uploaded through another browser or app. When an image is uploaded to a website, Brave sends a stripped copy and leaves the original file on the computer unchanged. The feature appears in the release notes for version 1.98.60 on 27 October, and the corresponding request was opened on Brave's GitHub in 2019.

The title and first paragraph of Brave's announcement mention Instagram alongside Facebook, but the tests and demonstration steps in it all use Facebook photos. As of 15 November we found no independent test showing that Instagram photos also carry FBMD. In the IPTC's 2019 table of social media sites, the Instagram row records only that the site offers no way to save or download images and that no embedded metadata was displayed.

Perspective

In both its 2016 and 2019 tests, the IPTC found two fields whose values differed from what was uploaded, and assumed Facebook had filled them in. The Job Id field got a new value with every upload, while the FBMD value in "Special Instructions" stayed the same when someone else uploaded the photo again. The IPTC states that it makes no assumptions about what these values are for, and in 2019 it could find no specification or statement from Facebook. Brave's announcement deals only with FBMD and does not mention Job Id, and the effect it describes is making it harder for Meta to link the same photo across accounts and sites, not preventing it altogether.

Other photo metadata has legitimate uses, such as photo apps sorting pictures by date and place. Brave lists removing location, device and date and time as features it would like to add later, and says users will decide when to remove them.

Brave uses Chrome as the comparison case without this protection. In 2012 someone filed a request in Firefox's bug tracker to delete EXIF data (the shooting details a camera writes into a photo) automatically on upload, and as of 15 November its status is WONTFIX. That request concerns EXIF, which is a different format from the IPTC field that holds FBMD.

People using Brave on desktop only need to update to 1.98 or later, and the announcement mentions no setting to turn on. The announcement includes steps to check. Save a photo from facebook.com in a browser such as Chrome, then open it in an image metadata viewer that runs in the browser, and the "Special Instructions" field shows a value beginning with FBMD. Open the same metadata viewer in Brave and choose the same file, and the value is gone.

When we checked on 20 October, GreatFire's last test in mainland China, on 18 October, had found brave.com 100% blocked, with interference recorded since 13 May 2017, and its most recent valid test of laptop-updates.brave.com, used for downloads and updates, was also blocked. On the same day, Apple's iTunes lookup API returned no Brave listing in the mainland China App Store (a lookup result, not an announcement of removal by Brave or Apple), while the Taiwan, Hong Kong, Japan, South Korea and Singapore stores listed Brave 1.96 (6 October). In none of those places does the App Store version bring this protection, since as of 15 November Brave has only announced plans for mobile.

Inferring from the two points at which the identifier is removed, saving and uploading, files that were neither downloaded nor uploaded through Brave on desktop are not protected, and neither are photos saved and shared through apps on a phone.

item.title: Tighter limits on outside contributions to open source projects in the AI era
item.dc:creator: Toomore Chiang
item.description: curl ended its bug bounty, and GitHub now lets maintainers limit who can open pull requests and issues; in 2026 open source projects are narrowing the ways outsiders can contribute. The author argues that this addresses the volume problem created by floods of low-quality submissions, but the trust problem remains. The malicious releases in both the xz backdoor and the Shai-Hulud worm were published from developer accounts that were already trusted, and what is missing is review capacity and permission management.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 23 sources, including curl author's blog, curl, GitHub

The source code of open source projects is still public, but what outsiders can send into those projects is increasingly restricted. By entry points I mean the channels through which outsiders send code changes, report problems or disclose vulnerabilities to a project. In 2026 one project ended its bug bounty (a programme that pays people who report vulnerabilities) and the code hosting platform GitHub began letting maintainers reserve proposed changes for collaborators (members a project has added and who can change its code directly), in both cases for reasons that had to do with the flood of submissions that AI has brought. I want to work out what tightening these entry points protects, and what open source projects pay for it.

My view is that closing off outside PRs (pull requests, proposed code changes submitted to a project) can hold back the flood of low-quality contributions that AI sends in, and the projects tightening their entry points mostly justify it as protecting maintainers' time. Tightening addresses a problem of volume, and the trust problem remains. I believe supply chain attacks (planting malicious code in software that others depend on, so that it reaches users through updates) mostly come in through accounts or people who are already trusted, and what open source projects really lack is review capacity and permission management. What worries me is that tightening gets treated as a security measure; in its announcement that it was shutting down, Jazzband, an organisation that jointly maintained Python packages, tied open membership to whether it could operate safely.

Now that AI tools make producing code fast and easy, review capacity has become the bottleneck, so I think open source projects should adjust how they think about contribution. When a project receives a change, a maintainer first has to understand the code and check it for errors and security problems before merging it, and this step is called review. Reviewing other people's changes, writing tests that reproduce a problem and describing a problem clearly have always been important parts of maintaining a project, and until now maintainers have mostly done that work themselves. With more code arriving, I think outside contributors need to share this work, and it should be recognised as contribution.

Tighter entry points for outside contributions

The author of curl, a widely used network transfer tool, announced on their blog on 26 January that the project's bug bounty was ending, and it officially stopped on 31 January. According to the same post, the programme confirmed 87 vulnerabilities in total over its run from April 2019, and paid out more than 100,000 USD in rewards to researchers. The author wrote that the aim of ending the bounty was to stop giving people a reason to make up reports in order to collect a reward. Anyone who wants to report a vulnerability now uses GitHub's private vulnerability reporting feature or emails the project's security address.

According to GitHub's blog post of 12 February, maintainers could already limit opening PRs to collaborators, or turn PRs off entirely. From 17 June, per GitHub's changelog, maintainers can set the maximum number of PRs that any other user may have open at the same time. Once someone reaches that limit, they cannot open a new PR until an older one has been closed or merged.

Draft PRs do not count towards the limit, and maintainers can add trusted contributors to a bypass list. On 28 October GitHub added automatic exemption rules, which let people go over the limit if their account is at least a set number of days old or if they have already had a set number of PRs merged in that repository.

On 29 June GitHub extended the collaborators-only option to issues (threads for reporting problems or making requests), so a project can now allow only collaborators to open issues. According to the changelog, once this setting is on, nobody else can create an issue from anywhere in the repository. This change matters more to me, because I see issues as the main channel through which people who do not write code report problems.

Tightening is also showing up in projects' own contribution policies: Open Source Says No, a site that tracks AI contribution policies, listed 221 projects as of 20 November. To be listed, a project needs at least 5,000 stars on GitHub, or must be widely used infrastructure such as a distribution, a language runtime or a major library. Of these, 24 ban AI-generated contributions, and most of the rest accept AI-assisted contributions with conditions attached, such as disclosing that AI was used or having the work reviewed by a person. According to its about page, the site is informational only and takes no position on whether those policies are right.

The gap between the cost of creating and the cost of reviewing

According to GitHub's February post, a PR can now be generated in seconds, and generative AI makes it easy to produce code, issues and security reports at scale. In the post's words, "The cost to create has dropped but the cost to review has not." According to the same post, maintainers have always dealt with noisy inbound, and low-quality submissions are nothing new. The Linux kernel's contribution rules contain a similar passage: tools can increase the number of contributions, but the time of reviewers and maintainers is limited.

According to curl's author, in earlier years more than 15% of submissions to the bounty programme turned out to be confirmed vulnerabilities, and from 2025 the rate fell below 5%. The author attributes this to an explosion of AI slop, adding that even reports that were not obviously slop had dropped in quality, a decline that began slowly in the second half of 2024 and accelerated badly in 2025.

According to the same post, PRs have not been a problem for curl, because no human time needs to go into reviewing a PR until it passes all 200 CI jobs (continuous integration, the tests that run automatically on every change). I take this as an example of automated checks lowering maintainers' cost of verification: what curl tightened was the entry point for vulnerability reports, and PRs remain open.

On 31 May a maintainer of Home Assistant (an open source smart home platform) wrote on their personal site that AI lets contributors send more changes, but each one still has to be verified by a maintainer. As they describe it, a contributor used to have to understand the code, write the change, run the tests and explain the result before they could submit anything, and those steps were a hurdle in themselves. The test they propose is whether the person submitting a change understands it, has validated it and takes responsibility for it, and whether AI was used is not part of the test. As I read it, what matters in this test, as with curl's automated checks, is who bears the work of verification.

Risks that tighter entry points can and cannot prevent

In the documents I cited above, the reasons I found for tightening were the volume of submissions and maintainers' time, not protection against supply chain attacks. The Jazzband announcement mentioned at the start is the exception: it tied the open membership model to whether the organisation could operate safely, and cited the xz backdoor as an example of what happens after a lone maintainer burns out. That is why I consider tighter entry points alongside supply chain security.

I see these three measures (ending the bug bounty, limiting the number of PRs and letting only collaborators open issues) as responses to the volume of submissions, and I think they can ease the volume problem. curl's author also cautions that their guesses about ending the bounty may be wrong, and that if so they will take further steps. According to a report in The Register on 21 October, curl announced that week that it would move low and medium severity vulnerabilities into public view, and the reason given in the report is to protect curl's security team, which was "almost overwhelmed by AI-assisted reports". Judging from that report, the pressure from incoming reports remained after the bounty ended, and how much tighter entry points relieve it will depend on the numbers that follow.

xz is a compression tool common on Linux systems. Looked at from the entry-point side, the xz backdoor, exposed in March 2024, suggests that tighter entry points would help against this kind of attack, which differs from my view. The account that planted the backdoor started out as an outside contributor. According to the xz project's website, the release tarballs (compressed archives) of versions 5.6.0 and 5.6.1 contained the backdoor, and those two tarballs were created and signed by that same account.

According to a public timeline that cites the xz-devel mailing list day by day, the account sent its first innocuous patch in October 2021, and by the end of 2022 it was able to merge changes into the project directly. In February 2024 it hid the backdoor in binary test files and then released 5.6.0.

From that angle, if a project took no outside patches at all, this account could not even have taken its first step. Counting from the dates in the timeline, two years and four months passed between the first patch and the backdoored release. My view is that tightening entry points can only delay attacks in which someone spends a long time earning trust, and a patient attacker can still trade time for trust.

According to the message on oss-security, the open source security mailing list, that publicly warned of the backdoor, one portion of it existed only in the release tarballs: a line of build script that was not in the source on git. As I understand it, distributions and users often download tarballs that maintainers package separately and sign digitally, and their contents are not necessarily identical to the public source on git. So my inference is that even careful review of every PR would not have revealed that line, and that what matters is who has permission to create and sign release files.

The original maintainer wrote on the mailing list in 2022 that the effort they could put in was limited (as transcribed in the same timeline). I think the weakness the xz incident exposed is having too few maintainers, together with how the project managed who was given release permissions. Closing the entry points will not give a project one more person to share reviewing and releasing either.

Jazzband let anyone join, and its members shared push access (permission to push changes directly into a project); in March it announced it would gradually wind down, and it disabled new sign-ups. According to the announcement, over ten years Jazzband grew to 3,135 members and maintained 84 projects. The reason given in the announcement for winding down is that a flood of AI-generated spam PRs and issues made open membership and shared push access untenable. Its lead also wrote that they could not keep giving push access to everyone who joined while still operating Jazzband safely.

Another problem listed in the announcement is that every project transfer, PyPI (the Python package publishing platform) permission change and infrastructure decision had to go through the lead alone. In the same announcement, the lead describes xz as an example of a lone maintainer burning out and someone malicious filling the gap.

The immediate cause given in the announcement is AI submissions, but I see it as a permission management problem. At Jazzband, anyone who joined got push access and could push changes straight into the organisation's projects. Once junk submissions multiplied, I think the lead could no longer judge whether everyone joining could be trusted, and no one else was there to share that gatekeeping. Handing out access on joining therefore stopped being workable.

The Shai-Hulud worm, for its part, is a case of trusted accounts being hijacked. According to an alert from the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) dated 23 September 2025, this self-replicating worm compromised over 500 packages on npm (the JavaScript package registry). How the attackers first got in is not stated in the alert, whose account begins after that point: the malware searched the environment for stored credentials, targeting GitHub tokens (keys that let a program sign in to an account in place of a password) and keys for cloud services. The worm then signed in to npm as the compromised developers, added malicious code to other packages and published new versions of them.

Among the recommendations in CISA's alert are rotating all developer credentials and requiring phishing-resistant multifactor authentication (a second check at login besides the password) on GitHub and npm accounts. None of the recommendations in the alert is to restrict outside PRs. I think the xz attacker traded time for trust, while Shai-Hulud scanned for and stole developer credentials and published as the compromised developers; in both cases the damage was done through accounts that were already trusted. The difference is that the xz account spent time building up trust of its own, while Shai-Hulud stole the trust that other developers had already built up.

Sources of new maintainers

According to GitHub's February post, these restrictions can disproportionately affect first-time contributors acting in good faith, which is why GitHub made them optional, configurable settings. My inference is that a newcomer who does not meet the automatic exemption rules has to wait for a maintainer to add them to the bypass list by hand before they can go over the cap on open PRs.

In September two software engineering researchers posted a paper on arXiv (a preprint platform for academic papers). According to the abstract, AI has made it cheaper to write a change, while reviewing someone else's contribution still takes comparatively more effort. Some projects have therefore restricted who may submit code, while still welcoming other kinds of participation. The authors argue that these projects impose the restriction not because the code was written by AI, but because such code is no longer worth the effort of reviewing.

The researchers call this form a stewardship community. In this kind of community, only a small group of core members can put code into the project, while other people can still shape the software without writing code. By the paper's definition, writing code there increasingly requires approval first, rather than being something contributors can start on their own. The authors also caution in the abstract that AI can replace the coding work that outside contributors used to supply, while weakening how open source communities renew themselves (by bringing in new members who can take over).

In another paper posted on arXiv in October, its authors reviewed 50 grey literature documents (blog posts, announcements and other material not published through academic channels) from 31 organisations or individuals. According to the abstract, most responses kept pull requests in some form while adding tools or restrictions, and restriction was the response most often reported as adopted. My inference is that, with tightening entry points already the most common response, more and more projects will run into the question of where new maintainers will come from.

I expect that once entry points are tightened, projects will find it harder to develop new maintainers from among outside contributors, and the shortage of maintainers will persist. I see this cost as the same weakness xz had: an attacker only has a gap to fill because there are too few maintainers.

A shift in what counts as contribution, and signals for readers

Some people see closing the door as going against the spirit of open source. A maintainer of the AI agent tool goose wrote on their blog in February that "Closing the door on contributors isn't the answer" and that "we can't give up on the thing that makes open source special", arguing that projects should spell out the bar for contributions and let CI check it automatically. In a survey of maintainers that Tidelift ran after the xz incident in 2024, one respondent likewise said that "Trusting new maintainers by default is the open source way, and how it should remain."

I see it differently: people mean different things by "the spirit", and what can serve as a shared baseline is the Open Source Definition. Published by the Open Source Initiative, the definition sets conditions on the licence, such as free redistribution, access to the source code and the right to modify it, and does not require a project to accept outside contributions. The official documentation of both SQLite and Lua calls them open source, yet SQLite only accepts patches from people who have signed an affidavit dedicating their contribution to the public domain, and Lua asks people not to send pull requests. I think the licence guarantees that everyone can take the code and change it, while each project can decide its governance according to the people it has.

I am not against projects tightening their entry points; facing a flood of submissions, maintainers need to protect their time first. I hope the time saved goes into review and permission management, such as who can merge, who can release and how tokens are kept, and the CISA recommendations mentioned above can serve as a starting point for that check. The goose maintainer's suggestion, spelling out the bar for contributions and letting CI check it automatically, is also worth doing in my view, since it too lowers the cost of verification.

I think the work worth counting as contribution is work that lowers maintainers' cost of verification. The xz backdoor was found because a developer noticed remote logins over ssh using an unusual amount of CPU on the development version of Debian, a Linux distribution, along with errors reported by valgrind (a tool for checking memory errors). The developer traced the cause and posted a public warning on oss-security, and I see that message as a problem description worth no less than a patch.

Anyone who wants to get involved can start by reading a project's contribution policy. Among the policies collected by Open Source Says No, the Linux kernel's requires contributors to understand everything they submit and to be able to defend it. According to curl's contribution document, the project accepts code written with the help of AI as long as it meets the usual requirements on coding style, documentation and tests. Reporters who use AI tools to find problems also have to disclose this in their reports.

People who do not write code can take part too: when reporting a problem, writing down the version, the steps taken and whether it can be reproduced saves maintainers verification time. When a project limits issues to collaborators, check its contribution document first for other ways to report.

For people who use privacy tools, I suggest looking at how many active maintainers a project has, whether its contribution policy spells out rules on AI and permissions, and how long vulnerabilities take from report to fix (contribution documents, release notes and security advisories usually cover this). As of 20 November, Open Source Says No did not list tools such as Tor (the onion routing network), Tails (an amnesic live operating system) or Signal (an encrypted messaging app). The site only lists projects that pass a threshold of GitHub stars or breadth of use, so not being listed does not mean a project has no such rules, and that has to be checked in each project's contribution documents.

These signals are only a reference, and having more maintainers does not guarantee safety either. At the end of 2022 the xz README listed two maintainers (according to the same timeline), one of whom was the account that later planted the backdoor.

Does the contribution guide of the privacy tool you rely on say anything about AI or permissions? If the project stopped accepting outside PRs, how would you take part?
