item.title: Phrases excluded from iPhone keyboard suggestions and swipe typing
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: An independent researcher recovered a phrase list Apple has not disclosed from the keyboard data in iOS 27.0, with 4,513 English entries and lists for 27 other languages and scripts. Listed phrases do not appear in predictive text and most cannot be swipe-typed, while typing letter by letter is unaffected. Apple's reply to Reuters said the keyboard is set up to avoid suggestions that might be inappropriate or offensive, and as of 15 November its support page offers no setting to turn the list off.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 9 sources, including Apple, Reuters (via CP24), Swipeblocked

According to a Reuters exclusive on 6 November, an independent researcher found that the iPhone's built-in keyboard carries a list of phrases Apple has not disclosed. Phrases on the list do not appear in predictive text (the next-word suggestions the keyboard shows during typing), and most cannot be produced by swipe typing (entering a word by sliding a finger across the letters). Typing letter by letter is unaffected, and nothing on the list stops anyone from writing a word. The lists are kept per language, and the researcher's site says Apple keeps similar lists for 27 other languages and scripts, giving a few examples.

The researcher told Reuters that in September he noticed swipe typing stumbling over "white man" but not "black man". With the help of AI coding tools he traced the behaviour to data stored deep in the operating system, and he put a conservative estimate at about 100,000 words and phrases, not including Chinese characters. According to Reuters, an engineer at a security company said he had independently recovered the same list and got "a near-perfect match". Swipeblocked, the site where the researcher publishes the list, has 4,513 English entries and says many of the other languages' lists are as long as the English one.

The researcher told Reuters that the entries are overwhelmingly vulgar, offensive or related to drugs, sex or violence. According to Reuters, other phrases are "politically salient", and Swipeblocked's examples include "Tibetan independence", "United Ireland", "Kashmir dispute", "sleepy Joe" and "make America great again". "Taiwan is country" is also on the list, and the site notes that only this wording is blocked, while "Taiwan is a country" is not. Some pairs are blocked on one side only, so "read gay smut" is blocked and "read smut" is not.

According to Swipeblocked's explanation, predictive text never offers a phrase on the list, "even when it's the obvious next word". Swipe typing won't produce most of them either: the keyboard picks another word, sometimes an implausible one, and can change a word already entered. In the site's demonstration, swiping "conspiracy" after "left wing" turns "wing" into "wrong". The rules match exact word sequences, so a slightly different wording can get through.

Reuters tested a small subset of the researcher's phrases on an iPhone and found they were all difficult to swipe-type or were not suggested via autocomplete. Swipe-typing "United Ireland" often yielded "United Iceland", and "Sleepy Joe" yielded "Sleepy hope". "Dictator Trump" could be swipe-typed but was not suggested, and Swipeblocked likewise lists it among the phrases kept out of suggestions that can still be swiped.

According to Swipeblocked's changes page, the English list grew from about 1,700 phrases in iOS 14.0 in 2020 to 4,513 in iOS 27.0. Apple updates it with new versions of iOS and, in between, through language data the iPhone downloads in the background. "Dictator Trump" was added in iOS 16.1, while "President Trump" and "President Bush", blocked since a 2022 update, were removed in iOS 26.3. The only addition in iOS 27.0 was "Zionist propaganda".

In an email to Reuters, Apple did not comment directly on the findings, including the size or composition of the list or its reasons for flagging certain political terms. Apple's reply said that iPhone users have always been able to type specific words or phrases and override any predictive suggestion, and that the keyboard is set up to avoid offering suggestions that "might be inappropriate or offensive".

Perspective

Swipeblocked's technical write-up says that before the keyboard offers a candidate, the two to six words it would complete are checked against the list. The list stores only a 32-bit fingerprint of each phrase rather than its text, and the researcher recovered the contents by generating candidate phrases and checking each one against Apple's table. Fingerprint matching also produces false hits, with 176 meaningless strings in the iOS 27.0 English list matching by coincidence, and on an iPhone these are blocked just like real phrases. The site also notes that parts of the list could not be decoded, and that a phrase's presence "says nothing about why Apple added it".

Based on the keyboard code in iOS 26.3, Swipeblocked also describes a separate set of labels on single words. Words labelled vulgar are not suggested until the user has typed them three times, and words labelled offensive are never suggested.

Macworld's editor writes that "This isn't a censorship list", because typing individual characters always works, though it can slow down anyone relying on swiping or suggestions to type faster. The researcher described it to Reuters as "a very light-touch form of censorship", adding that "at the scale that Apple is operating, it only takes a light touch to have a big impact." The Reuters report states that the list is not a ban, and that because hundreds of millions of people worldwide use iPhones, Apple's choices about which words its keyboard suggests "could quietly shape how they communicate".

On disclosure and customisation, a senior counsel at the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF, a digital civil liberties group) told Reuters that if Apple is going to do this, "this is something users should be really well aware of and have some ability to customize", and that it "should not be secret". Macworld's editor still calls Apple's approach "overreaching" and suggests a keyboard setting that is on by default but can be turned off. Apple's reply as reported by Reuters says nothing about disclosure or settings, and as of 15 November the keyboard page on Apple's support site has no such option. The same EFF lawyer said that while a part of him found the list "creepy" and he wondered about Apple's judgment calls, he could see an argument for it as a way to curb unwanted or inflammatory suggestions.

On what goes on the list, the researcher told Reuters it was understandable that Apple wanted to keep users from accidentally sending obscene messages or inflammatory slogans. He also said there were inconsistencies in how Apple applied it, pointing to "read gay smut" and "read smut". Macworld's editor suggests that Apple's motive is "likely less about policing your speech than it is about avoiding lawsuits and bad PR".

According to Swipeblocked, words on the Chinese list still appear as candidates when typed in pinyin, but once one is picked the keyboard stops suggesting the next word. The site's Chinese examples include 六四 (June Fourth, the 1989 Tiananmen crackdown), 台独 (Taiwan independence), 刘晓波 (Liu Xiaobo) and 习大大 (a nickname for Xi Jinping); the name of the Kuomintang (KMT) is blocked in both the Simplified and Traditional Chinese lists, while the name of China's Communist Party is blocked only in the Traditional Chinese one. In one part of the Chinese typing engine, Apple's code also skips suggestions whenever a word is "taiwan" or "tibet" written in English. The site's explanation does not cover input methods other than pinyin, such as Zhuyin (Bopomofo).

Citizen Lab, a research lab at the University of Toronto, analysed Apple's filtering of product engravings in six regions in 2021 and found 1,105 keyword filtering rules. It concluded that "part of Apple's mainland China political censorship bleeds into both Hong Kong and Taiwan", and that it was "aware of no legal justification for the political censorship of content in Taiwan". A 2022 follow-up found that Apple had eliminated its Chinese political censorship in Taiwan but continued broad, keyword-based political censorship in Hong Kong. Engraving filters refuse a custom order depending on the region of sale, a different mechanism from the keyboard list, which only affects suggestions and swipe typing; Swipeblocked decoded that list by language and did not compare iPhones set to different countries or regions.

On the iPhone's built-in keyboard, typing letter by letter is unaffected by the list. People who swipe-type may want to reread a message before sending it, since the keyboard can change an earlier word (our suggestion, based on Swipeblocked's demonstration). According to the keyboard page on Apple's support site, Predictive Text can be turned off under Settings > General > Keyboard. As of 15 November the page offers no setting to turn off the list, and does not say whether swipe typing still changes words once Predictive Text is off.

The same page describes Text Replacement, which lets users set shortcuts that automatically become longer words or phrases. The iPhone User Guide adds that filling in only the Phrase field and leaving the Shortcut field blank keeps a word or phrase the user types from being replaced. Neither page says whether either method brings listed phrases back into suggestions or swipe typing, and we have not tested it. For writing a phrase on the list, the method Swipeblocked confirms is typing letter by letter, and Macworld's editor gives the cost as slower typing.

item.title: The TLS Middlebox experiment in OONI Probe and a survey on data collection
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: On 10 November OONI announced a TLS Middlebox experiment in OONI Probe for locating censorship equipment, and at announcement the apps supported only its default mode. An advanced mode, which could let others estimate the city a user is in, is available only in the command-line version and only to users who opt in. OONI is also running a survey until 10 December on whether users would accept the collection of more geographic and network data. Readers who neither run Probe nor use OONI data are not affected.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 7 sources from OONI, OONI, Centre for Internet & Society

On 10 November OONI (Open Observatory of Network Interference) announced on its blog a new TLS Middlebox experiment in OONI Probe, designed to find where on the network path the equipment that intercepts encrypted (TLS) connections for censorship sits. OONI Probe is software for measuring website blocking that anyone can run on their own network, and its measurements are published as open data. The experiment ships in the command-line version (the one operated by typing commands in a terminal), v3.31.0, and in the mobile and desktop apps, v6.3.0. At announcement the apps supported only the default mode, while an advanced mode that collects more data was available only in the command-line version, and only to users who opt in.

On the same day OONI published a survey asking users whether they would accept OONI collecting more geographic and network-level data, and how useful such data would be to them. The experiment announcement says OONI wants community feedback before adding the advanced mode to the app, which is the version used by most Probe users worldwide. The survey is open until 10 December, and the survey announcement invites readers to pass it on to other Probe users and to people who use OONI measurements in their work. Readers who neither run Probe nor use OONI data do not need to do anything.

A middlebox is a network device sitting between the user and a website that inspects or interferes with traffic. OONI's test specification says the experiment detects devices that block connections based on the SNI (Server Name Indication), the website name sent in cleartext when a TLS connection is set up. According to the announcement, the experiment came out of a research project on transit censorship, where traffic that neither starts nor ends in a given network is blocked as it passes through that network.

In the steps the announcement describes, Probe first uses traceroute (a tool that lists the routers packets pass through along the way) to map the path to a target server. It then sends requests for a control domain and for a censored domain to the same server, making the requests expire at different points along the path. From this OONI can tell where censorship begins and find the network location of the censoring device. The same data can also help show whether the device is deployed close to the user or in another network, or even another country.

For each router on the path, the default mode records three things: the country of its IP address, the AS (autonomous system, a set of networks on the internet run by one operator or institution) it belongs to, and the AS's organisation name. The announcement's assessment is that the default mode brings no new risk beyond other Probe tests and OONI's risk documentation, since a third party cannot do any analysis that identifies a user from routers' countries and ASes alone. The cost is limited usefulness, because a censoring device can only be confirmed in a country or network when it sits deep inside it.

The advanced mode also records each router's IP address and the round-trip time (RTT) for packets to reach each router and come back. The announcement says this exposes users to more risk than existing Probe tests. A third party could use the routers' timing and location to triangulate the city where Probe was run, and could work back from the path to the user's /24 prefix (a block of 256 IP addresses sharing the first three numbers). In the worst case, if only one IP address in that block was in use at the time, the user's IP address could be found as well.

The announcement also describes a more realistic scenario, in which a third party can estimate the user's city and network but would find it hard to single out a specific person. OONI's reasoning is that a network has many live IP addresses and many people in the same city run the test. Because of these risks the advanced mode is opt-in only. In return, it can locate a censoring device even when it sits on the boundary between two countries or two networks, and it allows censorship to be measured city by city, which the announcement says the OONI community has long asked for.

Perspective

OONI's data policy says OONI does not aim to collect users' IP addresses and takes steps to remove them from its measurement database. The router IP addresses and round-trip times that the advanced mode publishes are the research data OONI wants, and also the data a third party would use to work out where a user is. Our assessment is that the research value and the degree of exposure cannot be adjusted separately.

Another principle in the data policy is that measurements sent to OONI's servers are published, and OONI does not, as a rule, delete measurements unless a user's safety is at stake. We infer that measurements from users who opt in to the advanced mode will stay in data anyone can download, for the long term, and could still be used later to estimate cities and address blocks.

The data policy also lists the user's country code and the ASN (AS number) of their network as fields attached to every measurement, and neither can be opted out of on its own. Running Probe carries risk in itself: OONI's FAQ says Probe is not a privacy tool, and anyone monitoring your internet activity (for example a government, an ISP or an employer) may see that you are running it. The risks page says the potential risks of running Probe depend on the user's threat model (who they might face and what that party can do) and on the laws of the country they are in.

For an Asian comparison, OONI and the Centre for Internet & Society (CIS) in India published a report in July 2020 on TLS blocking on three Indian ISPs, ACT Fibernet, Bharti Airtel and Reliance Jio. The report recorded SNI-based blocking on both Bharti Airtel and Reliance Jio, and found that Reliance Jio also blocked TLS traffic depending on the web server involved in the handshake. According to the report, state authorities order ISPs to block websites under Sections 69A and 79 of the Information Technology Act without giving technical specifications, so each ISP is free to adopt its own method, and regulations under Section 69A require ISPs to keep certain blocking orders confidential. The report cites a study based on OONI data that found website blocking in India "varies primarily from ISP to ISP, rather than from region to region".

The data in that report dates from 2020 and does not describe the situation today. We, a community based in Taiwan, found no OONI report dedicated to TLS middleboxes in Taiwan, Japan, Singapore, Hong Kong or South Korea (checked on 15 November).

As of the 10 November announcement, the apps do not have the advanced mode, and people running Probe through the app do not need to change any settings for it. Probe users with views on OONI collecting more data, and people who use OONI data in their work, can fill in the survey before 10 December. The survey is hosted on Google Forms, the link is in the survey announcement in the source list, and the announcement asks readers to spend a few minutes on it.

Where running Probe could itself draw attention, the risks page describes choosing which tests to run in the app. The data policy also mentions a setting in the app to stop sending measurements, which keeps results from being published. Drawing on the FAQ, we infer that neither step stops someone monitoring the network from seeing that Probe is running. For command-line users considering the advanced mode, the cost is that their city and address block may be estimated, and once measurements are published they are, as a rule, not deleted.

item.title: The netiCRM provider's server breach and a client's copied donation database
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: NETivism, the Taiwanese provider of netiCRM, a donation and membership management system for non-profits, had an internal management server broken into on 9 November. The provider confirmed that data such as client organisations' contact names and email addresses was stolen. According to an iThome update on 13 November, one client organisation was also notified that its donation database had been copied. For other clients' donor data, iThome wrote that the investigation was still ongoing (as of 14 November). People who donated, joined or registered for events through an organisation using netiCRM can watch for notices from that organisation and for impersonation scams.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 12 sources, including iThome, GitHub, 全國法規資料庫

An attacker broke into the internal management server of NETivism, the Taiwanese company behind netiCRM, a donation and membership management system for non-profit organisations, in the early hours of 9 November. According to an iThome update on 13 November, one client organisation announced on 12 November that the provider had notified it that its donation database had been copied. The organisation's notice lists donors' names, email addresses, phone numbers, postal addresses and donation records as possibly exposed. As for whether other client organisations and the people who donate to them are affected, iThome wrote that donor data was still under investigation (as of 14 November).

iThome's report of 12 November ran under a headline saying no leak of donor data had been found so far, based on the provider's statement of 11 November. As iThome relayed it, the provider had by then confirmed the theft of client data it held itself, including organisation contacts' names and email addresses, service plans, billing data and customer support records. For donor and supporter data on the non-profits' websites, the investigation had not yet found signs of theft, and the report did not say which records the investigation examined. The news that a donation database had been copied appears further down the same page, relayed through two layers, the client organisation's notice and iThome.

The account of the intrusion comes from the provider's statement in iThome's report of 10 November. The attacker obtained a username and password for the provider's internal code management system, then exploited a system vulnerability to gain administrator access to a server, breaking in at 01:55 on 9 November (Taipei time). The provider cut off all of the attacker's connections to that server at about 03:30 and sent clients a security incident notice the same day. According to the client notice that iThome quoted on 12 November, the provider reported the incident to the Ministry of Digital Affairs on the afternoon of 10 November and filed a report with the Taipei City Police Department.

In its statement of 10 November, the provider treated the admin accounts of client websites and the email account settings used for sending mail as possibly exposed, and said admin passwords were stored hashed (a one-way transformation that cannot be turned back into the password directly). According to what a client organisation relayed on the evening of 10 November, the breached machine was the provider's internal technical management server, not the server holding donation records. By 11 November, the provider's statement was that this server had administrative access to other servers, so every client server was being checked and rebuilt. Client websites and the netiCRM service might be temporarily unavailable during the rebuild.

According to the provider's statement of 11 November as relayed by iThome, its clients are more than 500 non-profit organisations. The provider had isolated the affected systems, identified the point of entry and replaced all leaked keys, and had also scanned and updated every client's mail server. Rebuilding the official website neticrm.tw, an investigation with outside experts and monitoring each server for anomalies were still under way at the time of the report, and the provider said the outside security firm it contacted had no staff available to help for now. When we, a community based in Taiwan, fetched neticrm.tw with a script on 14 November, we received only a verification page, so every statement from the provider in this article is relayed through iThome or client organisations.

Perspective

According to its official GitHub page, netiCRM is a fork of CiviCRM (a relationship management system for non-profits developed since 2005), and its source code is public. The provider has offered it since 2011 as SaaS (software as a service, where the provider hosts and runs the servers and the system). Organisations do not have to run their own servers, and in turn the security of donor data depends on how well the provider protects its internal accounts and management servers (our inference).

According to the provider's statement of 11 November as relayed by iThome, the breached management server held the management system's code, parameters and data. The attacker could use the stolen code and data to go on to attack client websites and vulnerable servers, and at the time the provider was working on fixing the stolen code. Changing passwords and keys only blocks connections that use the old credentials; once the management system's code is out, flaws in the code itself also need patching (our inference).

According to iThome, the client organisation whose donation database was copied urged supporters to stay alert to phishing emails, unknown callers and impersonation scams. The claim that credit card data was unaffected comes only from that organisation's notice. iThome reported on 10 November that more than 30 organisations had issued warnings, telling donors to watch for suspicious calls and scam messages. To find out whether an organisation you donated to, joined or registered for an event with has been affected, check that organisation's own notices.

The fields that organisation listed as possibly exposed include phone numbers, addresses and donation records, so an impersonator might be able to tell a donor which organisation they gave to and how much (our inference). If a call or email from someone claiming to be from the organisation asks you to transfer money, give a credit card number or change a direct debit, you can hold off and call back on the number listed on the organisation's official website. Calling back is our suggestion, not something the sources say. It stops impersonated requests, but it cannot stop data that may already have leaked from being reused.

The provider gave organisations using netiCRM advice on two occasions. In iThome's report of 10 November, it advised changing the passwords of every admin account as soon as possible, reminding donors to watch for scam calls and messages, and notifying internal stakeholders. On 11 November it advised first telling donors and members on the official website or social media that online donations and event registration might be temporarily unavailable, and posting an anti-scam reminder at the same time. The provider also said some of the attack sources pointed to IP addresses at client offices and that it had notified those clients, without giving details.

According to the provider, whether to report to the regulator is up to each organisation, based on the applicable laws, its internal rules and its arrangements with the regulator. Those who are unsure can ask the regulator or a legal adviser.

Article 12 of Taiwan's current Personal Data Protection Act requires a government or non-government agency that violates the Act, resulting in personal data being stolen or leaked, to notify the people concerned by appropriate means after the facts are established. The article contains no duty to report to a regulator and no deadline. Amendments promulgated in November 2025 add a duty to report to the regulator when an incident falls within a defined reporting scope, with the effective date to be set by the Executive Yuan (Taiwan's cabinet), and as of 14 November the Laws & Regulations Database still listed that date as undetermined. A Q&A from Taiwan's Personal Data Protection Commission Preparatory Office says the current Act continues to apply until the amendments take effect.

As of 9 October 2026, if a similar incident happened in Hong Kong, the organisation holding the data would have no statutory duty to report it to the Office of the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data (PCPD), which treats notification as recommended practice. The PCPD's June 2023 guidance advises notifying the office and the affected people as soon as practicable, particularly where the breach is likely to cause a real risk of harm. Amendment proposals that would make breach notification mandatory and regulate data processors directly were still under government study at that date, with no bill published.

As of 9 October 2026, if a similar incident happened in Singapore, the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 would make a breach notifiable if it results or is likely to result in significant harm to an affected person, or affects or is likely to affect 500 or more people. A data intermediary, which processes personal data on behalf of another organisation, must notify that organisation without undue delay. That organisation then assesses whether the breach is notifiable, which Singapore's Personal Data Protection Commission (PDPC) generally expects within 30 calendar days, and if it is, must notify the PDPC within three calendar days of the assessment. Affected people must be notified only where significant harm is likely.

People who have not donated, joined or registered for events through an organisation using netiCRM do not need to do anything. For organisations that use netiCRM, the provider has confirmed that contacts' names and email addresses were stolen, so staff may also receive impersonation emails (our inference). As of 14 November, iThome had reported only one client organisation being notified that its donation database had been copied, and did not say whether other clients were in the same situation. Next to watch are the provider's full investigation findings and the outside experts' investigation, and whether other client organisations receive the same notice.
